General Introduction · Area: key facts from the book
  • India is the seventh-largest country in terms of area after Russia, Canada, USA, China, Brazil and Australia respectively. India has 28 states and 8 Union territories. Its total area is about 3287263 sq. km. (According to ISFR:

2023, 3287469 sq. km.) which is approximately 2.4% of the world's total land surface.

  • According to the census 2011, 17.5% of the world’s population lives in India. The latitudinal and longitudinal extent of India is roughly about 30 degrees, whereas the actual distance measured from the north to south extremity is 3214 km and that from east to west is 2933 km.
  • As per the census of 2001, there were 6,38,588 villages in India, but after the 2011 census, the number rose to 6,40,932. India’s territorial limit extends towards the sea up to 12 nautical miles (about

22.2 km) from the baseline.

General Introduction · Latitudinal & Longitudinal Expansion: key facts from the book
  • Latitudes are the imaginary lines drawn by joining all the points having similar equal distance on the earth’s surface, measured in degrees from the center of the earth. 0º latitude i.e the equator, divides the earth into two equal parts. The equator lies midway between the poles. All of these lines are parallel to each other and are therefore called parallels of latitude, and on the globe are circles, becoming smaller polewards.
  • North and South poles are 90ºN and 90ºS latitudes respectively. Between these points, lines of latitudes are drawn at intervals of 1º. There are 89 parallels in the northern hemisphere and 89 in southern. So total number of parallels, including the equator is 179 (89 + 89 + 1). North of the equator is called as the Northern Hemisphere and south of the equator is known as the Southern Hemisphere. The distance between two consecutive latitudinal lines is approximately 111 km.

longitudinal lines Greenwich Meridian

  • The imaginary lines on the earth's surface joining the north and south poles crossing the equator are known as lines of longitudes. Such lines are also called meridians.
  • Unlike the equator which is centrally placed between the poles, any meridian could have been taken to begin the numbering of longitude. It was finally decided by an international agreement in 1884 that the zero meridian will be the one which passes through the Royal Astronomical Observatory at Greenwich near London. Zero meridians is also called the prime meridian or Greenwich Mean Time.
  • The longitudinal lines are not parallel to each other. The distance between two longitudinal lines is maximum at the equator (111.33 km).
  • East of the Prime Meridian is known as the Eastern Hemisphere and west of the Prime Meridian is known as the Western Hemisphere.
  • The 180º longitude is known as the International Date Line. India completely lies in the northern hemisphere.
  • The mainland extends between the latitudes 8º4' and 37º6' North and longitudes 68º7'E and 97º25'E. The southernmost boundary of Indian territory extends up to 6º45'N. The southern part of India lies within the tropics and the northern part lies in the subtropical zone or the warm temperate zone.
General Introduction · India and the Tropic of Cancer: key facts from the book
  • The Tropic of Cancer (23º30'N) divides India into almost two equal parts. It passes through eight Indian states: Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram.

The duration of the days increases with the northward movement of the sun. The position of the sun on 21 June is vertically overhead the Tropic of Cancer.

General Introduction · Standard Time: key facts from the book
  • To avoid difficulties a system of standard time is observed by all countries. Most countries adopt their standard time from the central meridian of the countries.
  • There is a general understanding among the countries of the world to select the standard meridian in multiples of 7º30' of longitude. That is why 82º30'E has been selected as the Standard Meridian of India. This meridian passes through the Mirzapur district (near Allahabad now Prayagraj) in the state of UP.
  • Indian Standard Time (I.S.T.) is 5 hours and 30 minutes ahead of Greenwich Mean Time (G.M.T.).

Indian Standard Time Meridian

East longitude Mirzapur

Madhya

Pradesh

Odisha

  • Standards Meridian of India passes through a total of5 states which are Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and Andhra Pradesh.
  • There are a total number of 360 longitudes. Only the Equator is a great circle dividing Earth into two equal halves; meridians are semi-circles and opposite meridians together complete a circle; other parallels form small circles. Since the earth rotates 360o in about 24 hours, which means 15o in an hour or 1o in four minutes. Therefore the difference in every 15º longitude is 1 hour. The earth rotates from west to east, so every 15º we go eastward, the local time is advanced by an hour and vice versa.
  • The whole world has been divided into 24 standard time zones, each of which differs from the next by 15º in longitude or one hour in time. A traveler going eastward of the Greenwich gains time (He will be 12 hours ahead of G.M.T. until he reaches the 180ºE meridian)m while moving westward he loses 12 hours when he reaches 180º W. There is thus a total difference of 24 hours on the two sides of 180º meridian. Thus the date changes exactly by one day when crossing the International Date Line. It is curved from the normal 180º meridian at the Bering Strait, Fiji, Tonga and other islands to prevent confusion of date.
General Introduction · Extreme Points: key facts from the book
  • India is located in the Northern Hemisphere. In India, the easternmost State/UTs is Arunachal Pradesh, the westernmost is Gujarat, the northernmost area is Ladakh (the then Jammu and Kashmir bifurcated into two UTs, i.e., Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh), and the southernmost is Andaman and Nicobar Islands. The four extreme points of India are-
  • Southernmost Point - Indira Point of Great Nicobar (6° 4'N latitude) is a village in the Nicobar district of Andaman and Nicobar Islands, India. It is the location of the southernmost point of the India’s territory. Kanyakumari (8° 4'N latitude) is the southernmost point on the mainland.
  • Northernmost Point - At Indira Col near Siachen Glacier in Ladakh.

  • When it is midnight at IST meridian, a place observes 6 A.M. The meridian on which the said place is located is-172° 30' E

Midnight at IST meridian (82°30'E), 6 a.m. at a place → it is 90° east (15° = 1 hour) → 172°30'E.

  • If it is 10.00 a.m. IST, then what would be the local time at Shillong at 92° E longitude?10:38 a.m.

10:00 a.m. IST → Shillong (92°E): 92 − 82.5 = 9.5° × 4 minutes = 38 minutes ahead → local time 10:38 a.m.

    General Introduction · Bordering Countries: key facts from the book
    • The neighbouring countries of India are Pakistan, Afghanistan, China, Nepal, Bhutan, Myanmar, Bangladesh, Maldives and Sri Lanka. India has natural as well as man-made boundaries. The Indian land boundary touches China and Nepal in the north, Afghanistan in the northwest, Pakistan in the west, Bangladesh and Myanmar in the east and Bhutan in the northeast. The border of India with Pakistan Afghanistan, China and Bangladesh is man-made.
    • Indian States & UTs sharing boundaries with neighbouring countries are

    Pakistan - Ladakh, Jammu & Kashmir, Punjab, Rajasthan and Gujarat.

    Afghanistan - Ladakh

    China - Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh.

    Bangladesh - Mizoram, Tripura, Assam, Meghalaya and West Bengal.

    Myanmar - Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur and Mizoram. Myanmar is also called as the land of Golden Pagoda.

    Nepal - Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal, and Sikkim.

    Bordering countries of India

    Shortest International boundary

    of India

    anLadakhChina
    PaPunjabUttarakhandSikkim

    Bhutan - West Bengal, Sikkim,Arunachal Pradesh and Assam. Bhutan is also called as the land of The Thunder Dragon.

    • The Himalayas in the north, Bay of Bengal in the southeast, Indian Ocean in the south and Arabian Sea in the southwest are the natural boundaries of India.
    • The boundary between India and Pakistan is an example of a superimposed boundary. A superimposed boundary is a boundary that has been imposed over an area by an outsider or conquering power. In 1947, India and Pakistan were separated through a draft created by a Britisher, Sir Cyril Radcliffe, and that is why the boundary line between India and Pakistan is known as Radcliffe Line.
    • The McMahon Line separates India from China. Afghanistan is separated from India by Durand Line.
    • In the sea, Sri Lanka is the nearest neighbour of India. Sri Lanka is separated from India by a narrow channel of sea known as the Palk Strait and Gulf of Mannar. The Palk Strait was named after the then Governor of Madras Robert Palk (1763-67).
    • Bangladesh forms the most extended land frontier (4096.7 km) with India. Afghanistan forms the shortest land frontier (106 km) with India.
    • The Eastern hills or Purvanchal are the southward extension of the Himalayas (Arakan Yoma, Naga Hills, Patkaibum) and form the land boundary separating Myanmar from India by the Irrawaddy River. The state of Tripura is surrounded by Bangladesh on three sides. Sikkim shares its boundary with three countries, i.e., Nepal, Bhutan and China. West Bengal shares its boundary with Nepal, Bhutan and Bangladesh.
    Physical Divisions: key facts from the book

    i. Natural Regions of India

    • Paleomagnetism is the branch that studies the magnetic properties preserved in the rocks, sediments or other such things during their formation. This branch of science is helpful in the study of ancient geological phenomena. According to continental drift theory, the Indian mainland is a part of Gondwanaland. Gondwanaland includes present day Peninsular India, Australia, Africa, Arabian Peninsula, South America and regions of Antarctica.
    • In the mid Mesozoic era (Jurassic Period, 144-208 Million Years Ago), Gondwanaland split into a number of pieces through convection currents. The Indian plate started drifting towards north after splitting from Gondwanaland. Consequently, the Indian plate, moving towards north, collided with a bigger plate, called the Eurasian plate.

    Due to this collision, the sedimentary rocks of the Tethys Sea, between the two plates (i.e., Indian and Eurasian), folded and developed into the Himalayas and mountain ranges of West Asia. The whole mountain range of the Himalayas represents a youthful topography. It has high peaks, deep valleys (gorges), and fast - flowing rivers. In the Terai region of the Himalayas, artesian wells are also found.

    • Due to upliftment of Tethys Sea in the Himalayas and the subsidence of the northern flank of the peninsular plateau, resulted in the formation of a large basin. With the passage of time, this basin was gradually filled with sedimentary deposits of rivers flowing from Northern mountains and Peninsular Plateau. In this way, a vast land area of alluvial deposits was developed as the ‘Northern Plain’ of India.
    • Geologically, Peninsular Plateau is the ancient part of Earth’s surface.
    • Peninsular Plateau is the most stable region of India. Peninsular Plateau comprises of hills and broad valleys which are made up of igneous and metamorphic rocks. Meghalaya plateau is an extension of Peninsular plateau. It was separated from Indian Peninsula through Malda Gap due to faulting. The Western Coast of India was formed due to faulting and subsidence of the western flank of the plateau.
    • The Indian mainland shows a large variation in the physical structure. Therefore India is divided into four natural regions. These are - 1. Northern Mountains 2. Northern Plains 3. Peninsular Plateau and 4. Coastal Plains & Islands.
    • Based on the variations in its geological structure and formations, India can be divided into 3 primary and 6 sub-physical geomorphic regions
    1.The Northern and North-Eastern Mountains.
    2.The Northern Plain
    3.The Indian Desert
    4.The Peninsular Plateau
    5.The Coastal Plain
    6.The Islands

    Highlands

    Physical Divisions · Northern Mountainous Region: key facts from the book

    Himalaya is the highest mountain range in the world.

    • Himalaya spreads to a length of 2500 km and from East to West. Its width varies between 160-400km. from North to South. We see more variation in Himalayan heights in the western part than in the eastern region.
    • Himalayas can be divided into 3 parallel structural regions

    1. Great Himalaya (Himadri)

    2. Middle Himalaya (Lesser Himalaya)

    3. Outer Sub-Himalaya (Shiwalik)

    • Great Himalaya is the oldest range, formed in the Eocene and Oligocene epochs (37-24 million years ago). Afterwards, the middle Himalaya was formed in the Miocene epoch (24- 5 Million years ago) and the Shivalik, the earliest one, was formed in the Pliocene epoch (5-2 million years ago).
    • Mountain Range situated in the northern part of the Himalayas is called the Greater or Higher Himalayas or Himadri. It is the most continuous range which has the highest peaks with an average height of 6000 meters.

    Northern and North - Eastern Mountains

    • Mt. Everest is the highest peak in the world located in the Great Himalayas. It is situated on the boundary of Nepal and Tibet.
    • Kanchenjunga, the third highest peak in the world, lies in the Himalayas. It lies between the Teesta River in the east and the Tamur River in the west. Kanchenjunga lies on the border of eastern Nepal and the Sikkim state of India.
    • Annapurna Peak is located in north - central Nepal. Dhaulagiri Peak also lies in the Western Part of Nepal. The core of this part of the Himalaya is made up of Granite. This range is always covered with snow. The Himalayas contain a number of Glaciers, therefore Himalayan Rivers are perennial. Ranges situated in the south of the Great Himalaya are called Lesser Himalaya/ Middle Himalaya. Its height lies between 3700 meters to 4500 meters and the average width is 50 km. Pir Panjal is the longest range in the Middle Himalayas. Dhauladhar and Mahabharat ranges are also important. Kashmir, Kangra and Kullu valleys of Himachal Pradesh are located in this range.
    • The outermost range of the Himalayas is called Shiwaliks. Its width is between 10 to 50 km and height between about 900m to 1100m. These ranges are formed by - unconsolidated sediments brought by rivers from main Himalayan ranges.
    • The longitudinal valleys lying in between the Lesser Himalaya and the Shiwaliks is known as Duns.
    • Some famous Duns are - Dehradun, Kotlidun and Patlidun.
    • The plain that lies in the foothills of The Shiwaliks sand longitudinally between the Indus in the west and Teesta in the east is called Bhabar. Bhabar is a narrow belt of land about 8 to 16 km wide covered with pebbles deposited by the rivers and lying parallel to the slopes of the Shiwaliks.
    • It is an alluvial fan structure made of riverine deposits. The width of the Bhabar plain is greater in the west than in the east.
    • Tarai is a 15-30 kilometer wide marshy area south of Bhabar. The Trans Himalaya is located to the north of Great Himalaya. Pamir knot is located in the Pamirs of Central Asia. The Karakoram mountain range is a part of Trans Himalaya. The Kailash mountain a holy shrine of Hindu religion, also lies in the western part of the Trans - Himalaya.
    • Himalaya is divided into various sub-regions from west to east. These divisions are based on the borders of river valleys. The Kashmir/Punjab/Himachal Himalayas lie between Indus and Sutlej rivers. The Kumaon Himalaya lie between Satluj and Kali rivers. Nepal Himalaya lies between Kali and Teesta rivers. Assam Himalaya lies between Teesta and Dihang rivers.
    • Brahmaputra River forms the easternmost boundary of Himalaya. Beyond the Dihang George, the Himalayas bend sharphy and spread along the eastern boundary of India. These expansions are called Purvanchal or Eastern Hills. These are located in North-Eastern states of India.

    The eastern extension of Himalaya includes Dafla hills, Mishmi hills, Abor hills, Patkai hills, Naga hills, Mizo hills and Manipur hills.

          Physical Divisions · Mountain Ranges and Hills of South and Central India: key facts from the book
          • The Peninsular Plateau is a tableland composed of old crystalline igneous and metamorphic rocks. Delhi Ridge in the northwest (extension of Aravallis), the Rajmahal Hills in the east, Gir Range in the west and Cardamom Hills in the south constitute the outer extent of the Peninsular Plateau. Shillong and Karbi-Anglong Plateau seen in the north east is a part of the Peninsular Plateau.
          • This Plateau was formed due to the breaking and drifting of the Gondwana land. Broad and shallow valleys and rounded hills are its special features.
          • It has two broad divisions, namely, the Central Highlands and the Deccan Plateau.
          • The part of Peninsular Plateau lying to the north of the Narmada river covering a major area of the Malwa Plateau is known as the Central Highlands. The Vindhyan Range is bounded by the Central Highlands in the South and Aravallis on the north west. The Aravalli range is the oldest mountain range in India, running across Rajasthan from northeast to southwest direction, extending approximately 800km. The northern end of the range continues as isolated hills and rocky ridges into Haryana, ending near Delhi. It is formed in the Pre Cambrian era. Its highest peak is Guru-Shikhar (1722m) located in Mt. Abu. It is an example of residual mountains. Residual mountains are remnants of old mountains that have been worn down by agents of denudation. The examples of residual mountains are Vindhyachal, Aravalli, Satpura, etc.
          • The Deccan Plateau is a triangular landmass that lies to the south of the river Narmada. The Deccan Plateau is higher in the west and slopes gently eastwards. It is bordered by the Western Ghats in the west, the Eastern Ghats in the east and the Satpura, the Maikal range and the Mahadeo hills in the north. The Satpura range forms the northernmost boundary of the Deccan Plateau. It lies between the Narmada River in the north and the river Tapi in the south. It spreads across the states of Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Chhattisgarh. Dhupgarh is the highest peak of the Satpura range located in Pachmarhi (M.P.).
          • Western Ghats are locally known by names such as Sahyadri in Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka and Sahya Parvatam in Kerala. Western Ghats are comparatively higher in elevation and more continuous than the Eastern Ghats. Their average elevation is about 1,200 m with the height increasing from North to South. Anaimudi (2695m), the highest peak of Peninsular Plateau, is located on the Anaimalai Hills of the Western Ghats followed by Meesapulimala (2640m).
          • Nallamalla Hills lie between the Krishna and Pennar rivers of South India, stretching from north to south, parallel to the Coromandel coast on the Bay of Bengal.
          • Javadi/Jawadhu Hills are an extension of the Eastern Ghats spread across parts of Vellore and Tiruvannamalai districts in the northern parts of the state of Tamil Nadu.
          • Nilgiri Hills also known as Blue Mountains, is the meeting point of Eastern and Western Ghats. Doddabetta (2637m) is its highest peak.

          Mountain Ranges and

          Hills of India

          • Toda tribe of South India reside in Nilgiri Hills.
          • Anaimalai Hills is located on the borders of Kerala and Tamil Nadu. Its highest peak is Anaimudi. Nilgiri Hills spread across the states of Tamil Nadu, Kerala, and Karnataka. The Cardamom Hills are part of South Western Ghats located in the Southeast Kerala and South-west Tamil Nadu. It is called so because of large-scale production of Cardamom in the area. They conjoin the Anaimalai (Anamalai) Hills to the northwest, the Palni Hills to the northeast and the Agasthyamalai Hills to the South.
          • Shevroy Hills is located in Salem district in Tamil Nadu. It is a part of the Eastern Ghats. Yercaud, a famous hill station of Tamil Nadu, is located on these hills. Mahadeo Hills are part of the Satpura mountain range located in Madhya Pradesh.
          • Kaimur Hills extend from Madhya Pradesh through Uttar Pradesh to Bihar.
          • Garhjat Hills which is home to the Gond tribes is located in Odisha, Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand. Balaghat range, Harishchandra range, and Satmala Hills are located in Maharashtra. Ajanta range completely falls in Maharashtra. Ramgiri Hills is located in the Peddapalli district of Telangana. It is a part of the Eastern Ghats. Maikal range is the eastern extension of the Satpura range. It is located in Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh. Jindhagada Peak (1690m) is the highest peak of Eastern Ghats located in Andhra Pradesh.

                Physical Divisions · Mountain Peaks: key facts from the book
                • Mount Everest is the highest peak in the world. It is located in Nepal and China (Tibet). Its height is 8848m. Nepal and China jointly announced the new height of Mount Everest as 8848.86 meters. It is also known as ‘Sagarmatha’ in Nepal. Bachendri Pal was the first Indian woman to reach the summit of Mount Everest in 1984.
                • Mount K2 is also known as Godwin Austen, the highest peak of India and Second highest peak in the world. It is located in Karakoram range in Ladakh. Its height is 8611m.
                • Kanchenjunga (8598m) is the third highest peak in the world and the second highest peak of India. It is located in the Indian state of Sikkim and Nepal. Nanda Devi (7817m) is the fourth highest peak of India. It is located in Uttarakhand. This region has been declared as Nanda Devi National Park. In 1988, UNESCO recognized it a World Heritage Site of natural importance.
                • Guru Shikhar (1722m) is the highest peak of the Aravalli range. It is located in the Sirohi district of Rajasthan. Kamet and Trishul mountain peaks are located in the Indian state of Uttarakhand.

                Nanga Parbat GA°udstwenin Major Peaks of India

                • Gosainthan is located in Tibet near the Nepal borders.
                • Utakmand is situated in the Nilgiri Range.
                • Kodaikanal of South India is located in Palni Hills of Dindigul district of Tamil Nadu.
                Physical Divisions · Valleys: key facts from the book
                • A valley is a low area of land between hills and mountains, typically with a river or stream flowing through it. India is blessed with many valleys, famous for their scenic views and historical importance. Valleys in India are found both in Northern and Southern parts, however valleys are dominantly found in the Northern mountainous part of the country.
                • The Himalayas are formed of parallel fold ranges. The Kashmir Valley, Doon Valley, Kangra and Kullu Valley (Himachal Pradesh), the Bhagirathi Valley (near Gangotri) and the Mandakini Valley (near Kedarnath) are various valleys that lie in the lap of the Himalayas.
                • The scenic beauty of these places makes the valley a tourism hotspot.
                • The Kullu Valley of Himachal Pradesh lies between Dhauladhar and Pir Panjal Range. The Nelang Valley is situated in the state of Uttarakhand (In the district of Uttarkashi near Gangotri National Park). It is situated near India-china border. It was closed for civilians after the Indo-China war of 1962. It was reopened in the year 2015 for tourism.
                • The Markha Valley is a famous valley of Ladakh (UT). The Dzukou Valley is situated in the states of Manipur and Nagaland.
                • The Sangla Valley of Himachal Pradesh is surrounded on all sides by mountain peaks and the Baspa River flows through this valley. The Yumthang Valley which lies at a distance of approx. 149 km from the capital of Sikkim i.e. Gangtok is known for its rhododendron vegetation and other such green floras. The valley is also known for its ‘hot springs’. The Silent Valley of Palakkad and Malappuram district of Kerala is situated in the Nilgiri Hills of Western Ghats.
                Physical Divisions · Passes: key facts from the book
                • A Pass is a gap, or break, in high, rugged terrain such as a mountain ridge. A Pass is formed when a glacier or a stream erodes, or wears away, the land between the areas of higher terrain. Passes often provide the easiest routes for people to travel across steep mountain ranges.
                • A Pass is a connectivity route through the basin of a mountain or mountain ranges. In India a lot of passes are found in the Himalayan region and the Western Ghats. These passes often become an essential medium for connectivity via roadways and railways.
                • The Karakoram Pass is situated in the Ladakh UT.
                • The Burzil Pass provides a route between Srinagar and Gilgit. The Srinagar-Leh route passes through Zoji La Pass, which is situated in the Zaskar Range. The route from Kulgaon to Kothi passes through Pir Panjal Range.
                • The route from Jammu to Srinagar passes through Banihal Pass.

                Mintaka Major Passes of India Zoji La

                Pir Panjal

                Baralacha La

                Banihal

                Shipki La

                Mana

                Niti

                Lipulekh

                Nathu LaLaDiphu La
                BPangsau

                Palghat Gap

                • The Shipki La pass is situated in the state of Himachal Pradesh. It provides a route that connects Himachal Pradesh to Tibet.
                • The Baralacha La pass provides a route between Manali and Leh. Thang/Tanglang La pass is situated in the Ladakh region.
                • Mana Pass which is also known as Chirbitya La and Dungri La, is situated in the Himalayan region of the country between India and Tibet. Mana Pass located in the state of Uttarakhand, extends from the Nanda Devi Biosphere Reserve to Tibet. Lake Deotal which is the source of river Saraswati, a tributary of river Alaknanda is situated in the Mana Pass.
                • Lipu Lekh Pass situated in the state of Uttarakhand lies on the Indo-China Border. The route for the Lake Mansarovar and Kailash Valley passes through Lipu Lekh and Nathu La passes.
                • Nathu La Pass is situated in Sikkim. Nathu La Pass extends upto Chumbi valley of Tibet Plateau region of China. Nathu La Pass is also the third Border Trade Point between India and China the other two being Lipulekh Pass of Uttarakhand and Shipki La Pass of Himachal Pradesh. Post the 1962 India - China War, trade through the Lipulekh Pass (Uttarakhand) and Shipki La pass (Himachal Pradesh) was closed; official trade resumed at Lipulekh in 1992 and Shipki La in 1995, while the Nathu La Pass in Sikkim was re-opened for trade in July, 2006. during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, trade through these point was disrupted; in August, 2025, India and China agreed in principle to re-open all three border trade points.
                • The Jelep La pass, situated in Sikkim, connects the Eastern Sikkim to Lhasa (Tibet).
                • Bomdila pass connects Arunachal Pradesh (Western Kameng District) to Lhasa (Tibet).
                • Yang Yap pass is located in the state of Arunachal Pradesh. The River Brahmaputra enters India near this pass.
                • Diphu and Pangsau passes which are situated in the state of Arunachal Pradesh lie on Indo-Myanmar Border.
                • Tuju pass (Manipur) located on south-east region provides a way from Imphal to Tamu and Myanmar. The Bum La Pass is a border pass between China's Tsona county in Tibet and India's Tawang district in Arunachal Pradesh.
                • The Western Ghats extend from the mouth of the river Tapti in the north to the cape of Kanyakumari in the south covering 1500 km in landscape.
                • Thalghat situated in the state of Maharashtra, provides road and rail connectivity between Mumbai-Nagpur and Kolkata.
                • Bhor Ghat Pass also located in Maharashtra provides road and rail connectivity between Mumbai-Pune-Belagavi-Chennai.
                • Palghat Gap is a low mountain pass in the Western Ghats in Kerala, it connects Palakkad and Coimbatore the two main cities of South India. The pass is located between the Nilgiri Hills to the north and Anaimalai (Annamalai) Hills to the South.

                Some other important passes of India are -

                Chang La- Ladakh
                Bum La- Arunachal Pradesh
                Rohtang Pass- Himachal Pradesh
                Niti Pass- Uttarakhand

                Muling La Pass is a seasonal pass located to the North of Gangotri. It connects Uttarakhand to Tibet. In winter it gets covered with snow, hence at becomes inactive for traveling purposes.

                      Physical Divisions · Snow Lines and Glaciers: key facts from the book
                      • The altitude at a particular place above which some snow remains on the ground throughout the year is called a snowline. A glacier is a slowly moving mass or river of ice formed by the accumulation and compaction of snow on mountains or near the poles.
                      • Different areas of the Himalayas have different snowlines depending upon the differences in latitude, relief, precipitation, slope and local topography. However, the average snowline is found at a height of 5500-6000 meters in the northern part of the Greater Himalayas and between 4500 - 6000 meters in the southern part of Greater Himalayas. Approximately 37500 sq. km. area of the Indian Himalayan Region (IHR) is covered by about 9575 glaciers, which mainly descend from the Greter Himalayas (Himadri) and extend from Jammu & Kashmir - Ladakh to Arunachal Pradesh.

                      Hispar Glacier Biaf° Glacier Important Glaciers of India

                      • The most important glaciers of Himalayas are located in the mountains of Great Himalayas and Trans Himalayas. Glaciers are found in the Karakoram, Ladakh and Zanskar ranges.
                      • The glaciers of lesser Himalayas are small in size, however, the Pir Panjal and Dhauladhar ranges provide evidence of larger glaciers. The largest glacier of Pir Panjal range is Sonapani, which is situated in the Chandra Ghati of Lahaul and Spiti district in Himachal Pradesh.
                      • The Karakoram and Greater Himalayas consist of immense glaciers, Siachen (76.64 km), Hispar (61 km), Biafo (60 km), Baltoro (58 km) and Sasaini (17.85 km) are some prominent ones. The Chorabari glacier is situated in the state of Uttarakhand in the district of Rudraprayag in the Garhwal Himalaya region of the state of Uttarakhand, north of the famous temple of Kedarnath. The southern slope of this glacier is located to the north of the temple of Kedarnath at a distance of approx. 4 km. Due to melting of the Chorabari glacier, a glacial lake was formed, known by the name of Gandhi Sarovar.
                      • The Milam Glacier is located in the Kumaon region of Uttarakhand. It is the main glacier of the area and the source of River Gori Ganga. Glacier - which is larger Siachen or Sasaini
                      • According to UPPSC - Siachen (source - Geography of India, Ramchandra Tiwari).
                      • According to Allahabad High Court - Sasaini

                      Source - Bhautik Bhugol Ka Swaroop - Author Ravindra Singh

                      - Geography of India by V.S. Chauhan & Alka Gautam - Geography of India by K. Bharadwaj

                      Now the books are efficient enough as a source for determining the measurement of the glaciers while sources based on real surveys are available regarding the length and area of glaciers.

                      Sources such as -

                      1. Records of the Geological Survey of India (Vol. 63)

                      2. World Glacier Inventory.

                       Decoding to the records of Geological Survey of India

                      1. Siachen (L-45 miles)

                      2. Sasaini - (L-11 miles).

                       According to the Geological Survey of India (Vol. 63, Pg. - 260) - outside the poles the largest glacier is Fedchenko, situated in the Pamir Region, whereas Siachen is the second largest glacier. Even according to the various sources available on the internet Fedchenko is the largest glacier outside the polar region and Siachen is the second largest. Hence, according to this order Sasaini is way below in the table.

                       According to World Glacier Inventory -

                       Siachen - L - 76.64 km, area - 1056.42 km²

                       Sasaini - L - 17.85 km, area - 33.51 km².

                       According to W.G.I. even Zemu and Gangotri glaciers are larger than Sasaini.

                      Hence the claim of Sasaini being a larger glacier than Siachen is debatable.

                      Physical Divisions · Plateaus: key facts from the book
                      • The Indian peninsula was formed around 3600 million years ago. Before the Carboniferous period it was a part of Gondwana's land.
                      • In the Carboniferous period, coal was formed in the Damodar, Son, Mahanadi and Godavari basins whereas in Cretaceous period bulk of volcanic eruptions led to the formation of Deccan Traps.
                      • The Deccan Plateau is a part of Indian shield. It is made up of basaltic lava. The Deccan trap was started to form approx. 66.25 million years ago. The Peninsular Plateau consists of both broad and shallow valleys and round topped hills.
                      • The peninsular plateau is basically divided into two parts- The Central Highlands and the Deccan Plateau. The part of the peninsular plateau lying to the north of the Narmada river, covering a major area of the Malwa Plateau is known as the Central Highlands.The Central Highlands are broad towards the west and start narrowing down towards the east. The eastward extension of the Central Highlands is sometimes locally known as Bundelkhand and Baghelkhand.

                      Plateau of India

                      • The River Damodar Drains the Chotanagpur Plateau which is a part of central highlands. The Chotanagpur Plateau mainly extends from Ranchi in Jharkhand to Hazaribagh, Santhal Pargana division, Palamu, Dhanbad, East and West Singhbhum districts, Purulia, Bankura, West Medinipur district of West Bengal and Mayurbhanj and Sundargarh districts of Odisha.
                      • The Chotanagpur Plateau comprises various other plateaus of different heights. In the central western part of the Chotanagpur Plateau pats is found, which has a maximum height of 1100 meters. All around this Plateau steps are found and the sharp break in slopes are marked by steep scarps.
                      • The central highlands, consist of rivers like Chambal, Sind, Betwa and Ken which flow from south-west to northeast thus being a proving factor of the slope of the region.
                      • The Malwa Plateau (length - 530 km, breadth - 390 km) covers approx 150000 km² area of Peninsular India. Its borders are determined by Aravalli in the North, Vindhya range in the south and Bundelkhand Plateau in the east.
                      • The Deccan Plateau is a triangular landform, situated south of the River Narmada. The Satpura ranges flank its broad base in the north are Satpura Range while Mahadeo, Kaimur and Maikal ranges form its eastern extension. The Deccan Traps, where black soil or Regur is found which was formed as a result of weathering of lava (basalt) obtained by volcanic eruptions. Aravalli range is found in the Western and North Western parts of the Peninsular Plateau. The Aravalli Range is an eroded stub of ancient mountains and is the oldest range of fold mountains in India.
                      • A part of the Peninsular Plateau is also found in the northeastern part of our country. Locally they are called the Meghalaya Plateau, Karbi-Anglong Plateau and North Cachar Hills. This northeastern part of the Peninsular Plateau was separated from the mainland by Malda Gap due to faulting. There are three important hill complexes in the Meghalaya Plateau, named Garo, Khasi and Jaintia Hills respectively. The Dandakaranya region of Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Telangana, Maharashtra and Andhra Pradesh spreads across an area of 89078 km².
                      Physical Divisions · Coastal Regions: key facts from the book

                      (a) Indian Coastline

                      • India is surrounded by water on three sides. The length of the Indian Coastline is 7516.6 km. (According to data from the 1970s). As per MoPSW circular dated 29 April, 2025, the revised coastline length is 11098.81 km. The Indian coastline extends towards the Indian Ocean, dividing it into two sea: the Arabian Sea on the west and the Bay of Bengal on its east.
                      • India has a coastline that touches 13 States and Union Territories.

                      • The length of the coastline touching the mainland of the country is 5422.6 km (Now- 7870.51 km.) long. whereas the coastline away from the mainland is 2094 km (Now- 3228.3 km.) long.
                      • The state of Gujarat has the longest coastline whereas that of Goa is the shortest. The coastline or the seashore, is the area where land meets the sea or the ocean or a line that forms the boundary between the land and ocean, which is often called the ground line.
                      • The territorial waters of a country are known as its territorial sea. The range of the territorial sea of any country is measured from its coastline, towards the open ocean. Commonly it is somewhere around 12 nautical miles. India has complete and sovereign rights over this region. The contiguous zone extends 24 nautical miles from the baseline towards the open ocean. In this zone India has the right to collect customs duty and also carry out economic activities.
                      • The exclusive economic zone of any country extends 200 nautical miles from the baseline towards the open ocean. In this zone, India is allowed to conduct scientific researches.
                      Physical Divisions · Eastern and Western Coast: key facts from the book
                      • The western coastal area is a narrow stretch of a flat land that lies between the Western Ghats and Arabian Sea. The northern part of the western coastal area is called Konkan Coast (Mumbai and Goa) the central part is called Kanara Coast and the southern part is called Malabar Coast.
                      • The Eastern coastal area has developed as a result of deltas of rivers like Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri. Hence the Eastern coasts are very fertile. The region of eastern coastal area falling between Mahanadi and Krishna rivers is called Northern Circars.
                      • The Coromandel coast extends from Krishna delta in the state of Andhra Pradesh to Cape Comorin (Kanyakumari) in Tamil Nadu.
                      • The important harbors situated on the western coast are - Mumbai (Maharashtra), Janjira (Maharashtra), Udupi (Karnataka), Kochi (Kerala) and New Mangalore (Karnataka) etc.
                      • The important harbours on the eastern coast are Visakhapatnam (Andhra Pradesh), Haldia (West Bengal), Paradip (Odisha), Kamarajar (Tamil Nadu) and V.O. Chidambaranar (Tamil Nadu).
                      Physical Divisions · Islands: key facts from the book

                      (a) Island groups of the Bay of Bengal

                      • Among the island groups of the Bay of Bengal the Andaman and Nicobar Islands hold an important place. The Andaman group of Islands is separated from the Nicobar group of islands by a 10º (10 degree channel). The width of the channel is approx. 150 km, and it lies parallel to the 10º North latitude. The Andaman and Nicobar islands are a Union Territory located in between the Bay of Bengal and Andaman Sea. The highest peak of Andaman island group is Saddle Peak which is 732 meters above sea level. It is located in North Andaman Island near Diglipur.
                      • The highest peak of the Nicobar island group is Mount Thullier (642m), which is located on the Great Nicobar island. The Andaman and Nicobar island group consists of 836 islands (Islands/Islets/Rocky Outcrops).
                      • Barren Island, located in the Andaman Sea lies about 135 km, North East of Port Blair (Now- Sri Vijaya Puram). It is the only active volcano in South Asia and first erupted (recorded) in 1787. The Narcondam Island is also located in the Andaman Sea, which is a dormant volcano.
                      • The Andaman island group was formed as a result of the extension of the Arakan Yoma (a tertiary mountain range). Limestone, sandstone and shale are the most prominent rock features of this island group.
                      • In the Eastern coastal states of Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu, lies Lake Pulicat. The lake is famous for being the second largest brackish water lagoon in India after Chilika Lake. Sriharikota Island is situated near Lake Pulicat. The Island separates the lake from the Bay of Bengal.
                      • The Satish Dhawan Space Centre is located on this island and it is used by India for her satellite launch programme. The Adam’s Bridge (Ram Setu) starts as a chain of shoals from the Dhanushkodi, tip of India’s Pamban island and ends at Sri Lanka’s Mannar Island.

                            Physical Divisions · Island groups of the Arabian Sea: key facts from the book
                            • In Lakshadweep, near the Malabar coast lies an archipelago of 12 atolls, 3 reefs and 5 submerged banks with about 36 islands and islets. The name of this archipelago was changed to Lakshadweep in 1973, earlier it was known as the Laccadive, Minicoy and Amindivi Islands. The Lakshadweep Island lie about 220 km. to 440 km. off the coast of Kerala, with Kochi being the nearest major coastal city. Lakshadweep is a Union Territory with a total area of 32 persons/sq. km.
                            • There are 36 islands in the Lakshadweep Island group.
                            • The northernmost inhabited island of Lakshadweep is called Chetlat whereas the southern end is called Minicoy. Minicoy island is separated from the rest of the islands by 9° channels.
                            • Minicoy is the 2nd largest island (4.80 person/sq. km) of Lakshadweep.
                            • Kavaratti is the capital of Lakshadweep, located on the Kavaratti Island. The largest island of Lakshadweep is Andrott or Androth (4.90 km²). The Elephanta island is located near Mumbai about 10 km from the Gateway of India.
                            • Salsette island is in the state of Maharashtra on India’s west coast. The metropolis of Mumbai and the city of Thane lie on it.
                            • Offshore Island - from the deltaic regions of the Ganga to the Eastern and Western coasts of India, to Gulf of Mannar, many islands are located. Among these are Piram (Gulf of Khambhat), Bhainsala (Kathiawar), Diu, Baida, Nora, Pirotan, Karunbhar (Kutch), Kadiya Bet: Alia Bet (near the Mouth of the Narmada & Tapti rivers), Butcher (Jawahar Dweep), Karanja (Uran), Cross (near Mumbai), Pigeon, Saint Mary (near Mangalore), Anjediva (near Karwar Coast), Vypeen (near Kochi) Shortt Island, Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam Island (earlier Wheeler Island) near Dharma, Bhadrak on the Odisha coast, New Moore & Ganga Sagar (in Ganga Deltaic region) are some prominent ones.
                            • Niveshika is a tidal creeks. Sir Creek is a 96 km long tidal estuary in the Rann of Kutch region. It lies on the border of India and Pakistan and has been a disputed area between the two nations. It separates Gujarat from the Sindh province of Pakistan. The dispute lies in the interpretation of the maritime boundary line between India and Pakistan. At present the area is under the possession of India.
                            States/Union Territories of India · States: key facts from the book
                            • Presently India comprises of 28 states and 8 union territories. New Delhi is the capital of India. Presently, besides, National Capital Region (NCR) includes Delhi (Whole N.C.T.) and the sub-regions of Faridabad, Gurugram, Nuh, Rohtak, Sonipat, Rewari, Jhajjar, Panipat, Palwal, Bhiwani, Mahendragarh, Jind, Charkhi Dadri and Karnal districts of Haryana sub-region; Meerut, Ghaziabad, Hapur, Gautam Buddha Nagar, Bulandshahr, Muzaffarnagar, Shamli and Baghpat districts of Uttar Pradesh and, Alwar and Bharatpur of Rajasthan.
                            • According to Office of the Registrar General of India, Ministry of Home Affairs in terms of Geographical area five largest states in descending order of area are Rajasthan (342,239.00 sq.km), Madhya Pradesh (308252 sq. km), Maharashtra (307,713 sq. km), Uttar Pradesh (2,40,928 sq. km) and Gujarat (196,244 sq. km). According to Census, 2011 in terms of population, the four largest states in India are Uttar Pradesh (199812341), Maharashtra (112374333), Bihar (104099452) and West Bengal (91276115) respectively.
                            • Uttar Pradesh shares its boundary with eight states, one Union Territory - National Capital Territory of Delhi and Nepal. The eight states are Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, Haryana, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and Bihar.
                            • Currently Madhya Pradesh shares border with five states i.e. Gujarat, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and Maharashtra. Bhopal is the capital of Madhya Pradesh.
                            • According to the Andhra Pradesh Re-organisation Act, 2014, Andhra Pradesh shares a boundary with Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Telangana, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. Telangana shares borders with Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh. If the Yanam region of Puducherry is also taken into consideration, the number of states/union territories bordering Andhra Pradesh will be considered as six.
                            • Karnataka shares its boundary with six states - Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Maharashtra, Goa, Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
                            • Kerala shares its border with two states - Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. If the Mahe region of Puducherry is included the number of states and union territories bordering Kerala will be three. Tamil Nadu shares its border with three states - Kerala, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh including Puducherry the number of states / union territories will be four.
                            • Punjab shares its boundary with Rajasthan, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir and Union Territory of Chandigarh; and it is bounded on the west by Pakistan.
                            • Chhattisgarh shares its boundary border with Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha, Jharkhand, Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra and Telangana.
                            • The seven sister states in Northeast India consist of Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Meghalaya, Manipur, Mizoram, Nagaland and Tripura. Assam shares inter-state boundaries with seven Indian state- West Bengal, Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram, Tripura and Meghalaya and also has international boundaries with Bangladesh and Bhutan. Manipur state covers a 22,327 square kilometer area which is 0.7% of the total land area of India. The hill districts occupy about 90 percent (20089 sq. km.) of the total area of the state, while the valleys occupy only about one-tenth (2238 sq. km.) of the total area of the state.
                            • Phumdi are a series of floating islands exclusive to the Loktak Lake in Manipur state, in north-eastern India. They are made up of heterogeneous masses of vegetation, soil and organic matter in different stages of decay. According to ISFR, 2023 approximately 78.67% of the land area of Arunachal Pradesh is covered under forestry.
                            • Desert of Rajasthan is the most densely populated desert in the world, with a population density of 83 person/sq.km. It is about 10,000 years old. Here only 40% to 60% of the area is suitable for farming. Due to development of the irrigation facilities, there has been an increase in the net sown area which has adversely affected the extension of pasture area.
                            • Karnataka is known as the ‘Silicon State’ of India as it is a hub of information and technology companies. The Silicon Valley of India is a nickname of Indian city Bengaluru which is the capital of Karnataka. Malnad (Malenadu) is a mountainous region of Karnataka that is covered with dense forests.
                            • ‘Patland region is found in the Chota Nagpur plateau area. This area has High hilly peaks, and the maximum part of Chota Nagpur plateau lies in the state of Jharkhand.
                            • The world famous Kohinoor diamond was found in the Kollur mines of Andhra Pradesh. That is why this state is called as the Kohinoor of India.
                            • Vidarbha is the eastern region of the state of Maharashtra. Presently, there are two divisions in this region - Nagpur and Amravati. This region includes Nagpur, Amravati, Chandrapur, Akola, Wardha, Buldhana, Yavatmal, Bhandara, Gondia, Washim and Gadchiroli districts of Maharashtra.
                            States/Union Territories of India · Union Territories: key facts from the book
                            • Presently, India comprises of 28 States and 8 Union Territories.
                            • The 8 Union Territories are the National Capital Territory of Delhi, Chandigarh, Lakshadweep, Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu, Puducherry, Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh.
                            • The Andaman and Nicobar Islands are a group of islands at the juncture of the Bay of Bengal and Andaman Sea. The Union Territory of Andaman and Nicobar Islands is located at 6°-14º N latitude and 92°-94º E longitude.
                            • The area located to the north of 10ºN latitude is called Andaman island while the area to the south of10ºN latitude is called Nicobar Islands. The area of Andaman and Nicobar Islands is 8249 sq. km.
                            • Ladakh is the largest in area among union territories. The population of Andaman & Nicobar is 380581 (according to census 2011). Four Negrito tribes are found in Andaman Islands namely the Great Andamanese, Jarawa, Onge and Sentinelese. Port Blair (New name - Sri Vijaya Puram) is the capital of Andaman & Nicobar Islands.
                            • Chandigarh and its neighboring region became a union territory on November 1, 1966. This is the capital of both Haryana and Punjab. The area of Chandigarh is 114 km² and population is 10.55 lakh.
                            • Dadra and Nagar Haveli is surrounded by the states of Gujarat and Maharashtra. It has two parts. The first one is Dadra and the other one is Nagar Haveli. The area of Dadra and Nagar Haveli is 491sq.km and the population is 3.44 lakh (Census: 2011). Daman and Diu was a Union Territory of India. It has been divided into two parts Daman (on the Arabian Sea, along the coastal border of Maharashtra and Gujarat) and Diu (on the Saurashtra coast).
                            • Daman is the capital of Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu.
                            • New Delhi, the capital of India, and the National Capital Territory of Delhi, is a union territory. The area of the NCT of Delhi is 1483 sq. km and the population is 1.68 cr. (Census 2011).
                            • The NCT of Delhi, is the largest union territory in terms of population. Lakshadweep is the smallest union territory in India in terms of area (32 sq.km). Apart from this, the population of Lakshadweep is also the lowest (64473 persons) (Census 2011). There are 36 islands in the Lakshadweep. Kavaratti is the capital of Lakshadweep.
                            • Puducherry is divided into four separate districts, two of which (Karaikal and Puducherry) are situated near Tamil Nadu. Yanam is located near Andhra Pradesh and Mahe is located near Kerala.

                            The area of Puducherry is 490 km² and the population is

                            12.48 lakh (Census 2011). Puducherry is the capital of this union territory.

                                  Species/Tribes: key facts from the book
                                  • The Constitution of India has not defined the term Schedule Tribes. According to Article 366 (25) of the Constitution Scheduled Tribes means to tribes or tribal communities or parts of such tribes or tribal communities as are deemed under Article 342 to be Scheduled Tribes for the purposes of this Constitution. In India tribes are classified as per their cultural specialties, place of residence etc.
                                  • Tribal areas of India can be divided into 7 parts - (1) Northern Region,
                                  • (2) North Eastern Region, (3) Eastern Region, (4) Central Region, (5) Western Region, (6) Southern Region, (7) Island groups.
                                  • The Scheduled Tribes of India constitute about 8.6% of the total population of the country. The largest population of Scheduled Tribes is found in the states of Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Odisha.
                                  • As per the census of 2011, Punjab, Haryana, Chandigarh, the NCT of Delhi & Puducherry are the states and union territories where no notified scheduled Tribe is found.
                                  • As per the census of2011 the largest tribal group of India is Bhil, with a population count of17071049.
                                  • Gond is the second largest tribal group of India (pop. - 13256928). Santhals (6,570,807) and Naikda (3787639) are in 3rd & 4th place respectively.
                                  KJaamshmmuir LadakhScheduled Tribes
                                  D°ngra Ba(h)k(a)a(n)r(g)w(p)a(a)lof India

                                  Some of the important tribes of India are as follows

                                  Tharu - This tribe resides mainly in the Nainital district of Uttarakhand, particularly in the Khatima and Sitarganj Tehsils of Udham Singh Nagar district and the Terai regions of U.P. and Bihar. They believe in Hinduism. One unique feature of this tribe is that they celebrate Diwali as a sorrow. They live in joint families and are believed to be descendants of the Kirate clan. It is the largest tribal group in the state of Uttarakhand. Bhotia - This tribe resides in the hilly regions of Uttarakhand and the Terai regions of Uttar Pradesh among others. Bhotias belong to the Mongoloid race. The tribe is known for its migratory pastoralist nature.

                                  • Jaunsari - They reside in the state of Uttarakhand and Uttar Pradesh. They practice agriculture and polyandry.
                                  • Buksa - They reside in the Nainital, Dehradun and Pauri Garhwal districts of Uttarakhand and in some places in Uttar Pradesh. The Anulom and Pratilom styles of marriage are very prevalent in this tribe. The Buksa tribe claims to be related to the Rajput clan.
                                  • Raji - This tribe resides in Uttarakhand and Uttar Pradesh and practices Hinduism. Jhum cultivation is very prevalent in the tribe.
                                  • Kharwar - They reside in Deoria, Ballia, Ghazipur, Varanasi and Sonbhadra districts of Uttar Pradesh. They are known for their ill temper and strong physical features. The tribe is the second largest tribe of Uttar Pradesh.
                                  • Gaddi - The tribe mainly resides in Kangra and Chamba districts of Himachal Pradesh and is also found in Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir. The area falls in the Dhauladhar range of Western Himalayas. It is an ancient tribe of the Dhauladhar range having a population of over 1.5 lakh. They believe themselves to be descendants of Garhwa rulers of Rajasthan. Other prominent tribes of the Dhauladhar range are Gujjar, Bakarwal, Lahauli, Bari etc.
                                  • Gond - They are native to Gondwanaland hence they got the name Gond. The tribe is found in the states of Bihar, West Bengal, Jharkhand, Maharashtra, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Odisha, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Gujarat etc. For food resources, the tribe mostly depends on hunting and fishing though some shifting cultivation is also practiced. They were few clothes in their attire; however, women are very fond ofwearing ornaments. Animal sacrifice is practiced. The Gond is the largest tribal group in U.P.

                                  Bhil - The name Bhil is believed to have been derived from Villu or Billu, which in most Dravidian languages is the word for “Bow” in reference to the weapon that, until the desert times, they seemed almost always to be carrying.

                                  They belong to the proto-Australoid race, and are famous for their Ghoomar dance. They are found in the states of Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tripura, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Rajasthan etc. Santhal - The tribe is a native of Santhal Pargana hence they are called Santhals. As per the census of 2011, they reside in the states of Bihar, Tripura, West Bengal, Jharkhand, and Odisha etc. Their physical structure is very similar to that of the Dravidians. Rice is their staple diet.

                                  • Munda - The tribe resides in the states of Jharkhand, West Bengal, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Tripura, Odisha etc. The Munda tribe practices many festivals. Mage, Phagu, Karam, Sarhul and Sohrai are some of the important festivals. The festival of Sarhul is celebrated every year in the first month of the Hindu calendar, on the third day of the moon or the fortnight of'Chaitra' and is celebrated untill the month of June or 'Jeth.'
                                  • Korwa - Mainly found in the states of Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh and West Bengal. Mostly hunting and gathering is practiced though some of them practice agriculture too.
                                  • Kol - Found in the states of Bihar, Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra etc. the Kol tribe is mostly agrarian in nature.
                                  • Manganiyar - They reside in the desert regions of Rajasthan and practice Islam as their religion. They are known for their musical/folk legacy. They are also found in the Sindh Province of Pakistan.
                                  • Khasi - Found in the North-Eastern states of Meghalaya, Assam and Mizoram, the tribe practices Jhum cultivation.
                                  • Toda - They reside on the Nilgiri Hills, and are also known by the names Todi or Tuda. They claim themselves to be descendants of Aryans. They mostly practice pastoralism. Polyandry is prominent among the Todas.
                                  • Jarawa - It is the most primitive tribe of India. They reside in the Andaman and Nicobar group of Islands. Mostly found on the southern and Middle Andaman Islands their area of residence is protected by law in our country, hence human activity is completely prohibited in the region.
                                  • Onges - They reside in the western part of Little Andaman Island (Andaman & Nicobar group of Islands).
                                  • Shompen - The indigenous people of Great Nicobar, part of the Andaman & Nicobar Islands.
                                  • Sentinelese - Andaman & Nicobar Islands
                                  • Naga - The tribe resides in the states of Nagaland, Manipur, Assam, Meghalaya and Mizoram. They practise jhum (shifting) cultivation and are traditionally known for their distinct handwoven textile and shawls.

                                  Oraon, Ho, Bhumij, Kharia, Soura, Birhor, Khond, Kharwar, Asur, Baiga are some other important tribes of Jharkhand. Bhil, Meena, Garasiya, Sahariya, Damor and Pateliya are some other important tribes of Rajasthan.

                                        Languages: key facts from the book
                                        • The most spoken language in the country is Hindi. Bangla is at second place. In world rankings Bangla is in seventh place, spoken by almost 284.3 million people (Ethnologue, 2025). The various languages of the country can be grouped into the following -
                                        • Bharatiya European language family - Marathi, Sanskrit, Pali, English, Prakrit, Apabhramsa, Hindi, Bangla, Gujarati etc.
                                        • Dravidian language family - Telugu, Tamil, Malayalam, Kannada, Gond, Oraon etc.
                                        • Austro-Asiatic language family - Khasi, Santhali, Mundari, Bhumij etc. (these languages are mostly spoken by the tribal people of India).

                                        Drainage System: key facts from the book

                                        I. Ganga Drainage System

                                        • The Himalayan Drainage System comprises the most famous river systems of India i.e. the Indus, the Ganga and the Brahmaputra. Most of these rivers are perennial in character, obtaining water from the glaciers, springs and rains.
                                        • These rivers carve out a number of erosional landforms like gorges, waterfalls and steep-sided valleys, etc.
                                        • Ganga is the longest river (2525 km.) in India. The five confluences, known as the Panch Prayag, are all along the Alaknanda. They are, in downstream order, Vishnuprayag (Dhauliganga joins the Alaknanda), Nandprayag (where NandakinijoinsAlaknanda), Karnaprayag (where Pindarjoins Alaknanda), Rudraprayag (where MandakinijoinsAlaknanda) and Devprayag (where Bhagirathi joins Alaknanda).
                                        • The mainstream of Ganga begins at the confluence of Bhagirathi and Alaknanda in Devprayag. Ganga enters the plain area at Haridwar, flowing through the north of Rajmahal Hills, it finally enters Bangladesh by flowing through Farakka in West Bengal. In Bangladesh, it is known as the Padma. The Padma is joined by Jamuna (Brahmaputra). Further down stream, the Padmajoins the Meghna River. Here onwards the whole river system is known as the Meghna River system which drains into the Bay of Bengal.
                                        • The world’s largest delta (Ganga - Brahmaputra-Meghna Delta) is formed between the Hugli river and the Meghna river.
                                        • The important left bank tributaries of the Ganga are the Ramganga, the Gomati, the Ghaghara, the Gandak, the Kosi and the Mahananda.
                                        • The Yamuna is the right bank and the longest tributary of the Ganga. It has its source in the Yamunotri Glacier on the western slopes of the Banderpunch Peak. It joins the Ganga at Prayag (Prayagraj).
                                        • The Chambal, the Sindh, the Betwa and the Ken are the right bank tributaries of the Yamuna, while the Tons, Hanuman Ganga and the Sasur Khaderi are its left bank tributaries.
                                        • The Chambal River originates near Dr. Ambedkar Nagar (Old Name - Mhow) in the Malwa Plateau of Madhya Pradesh. It flows through a gorge. The Chambal is famous for its badland topography, which is called the Chambal Ravines. The Gandak originates from the Nepal Himalayas and joins the Ganga at Sonpur near Patna. The Ghaghra originates from the glacier of Mapchachungo. The river Sharda (Kali or Kali Ganga) joins it in the plain before it finally meeting Ganga at Revilganj (Saran, Bihar).
                                        • The river Ramganga joins the Ganga near Kannauj. The river Damodar flows through a rift valley and finally joins the Hugli. The Barakar is its main tributary. The Damodar River is known as the 'Sorrow of Bengal'. The Mahananda is the last left bank tributary of the Ganga joining it in West Bengal.
                                        • The Son is the major right bank tributary of Ganga. It originates in the Amarkantak Hill and joins the Ganga at near Patna (Bihar).

                                        Ganga

                                        Drainage System

                                        • The antecedent rivers are those streams that originate prior to the uplift of the land surface of an upland or mountain but maintain their original course of flow even after the landmass is uplifted, by cutting through the uplifted landmass. The Ganga river is an example of an antecedent river.
                                        • The Alaknanda has its source in the Satopath glacier above Badrinath.
                                        Drainage System · Brahmaputra Drainage System: key facts from the book
                                        • The river Brahmaputra originates from the Angsi Glacier near the Mansarovar Lake. Here it is known as ‘Yarlung Tsangpo’. It flows parallel to the eastward side of the Himalayas. It takes a ‘U’ shaped turn at ‘Namcha Barwa’ peak to enter in India. It enters India west of Sadiya town in Assam under the name of Siang or Dihang. Flowing onward, it meets its main left bank tributaries i.e. Dibang or Sikang and Lohit and thereafter it is known as the Brahmaputra.
                                        • Its major left bank tributaries in the Assam valley are the Burhi Dihing and Dhansiri whereas the important right bank tributaries are the Subansiri, Jiabharali, Manas, and Sankosh.
                                        • The Brahmaputra enters Bangladesh near Dhubri.
                                        • In Bangladesh, the Tista joins it on its right bank where the river is known as the Jamuna.
                                        • It finally merges with the river Padma, which flows into the Bay of Bengal.
                                        • The Brahmaputra has a braided channel along its entire length in Assam and forms many riverine islands. Majuli, the biggest riverine island in the world, is also the first island district of the country, located on the Brahmaputra River in Assam.
                                        • The Brahmaputra, the Satluj and the Indus rivers have their sources of origin near Mansarovar lake in Tibet.
                                        • The Tibetan Plateau is also known as the Qinghai - Tibet Plateau or the Qing - Zang Plateau. It is also called as the 'Roofofthe World'. (Note - The metaphor Roofofthe World usually refers to the mountainous interior of Asia, including the Pamirs, the Himalayas, the Tibet, the Tian Shan, and the Altai Mountains.) The Tibetan Plateau is the source of Asia’s major rivers such as Yangtze river, Huang He river, Indus river, Satluj river, Brahmaputra river, Mekong river and Salween river.

Of these rivers, Brahmaputra makes a “U” turn in its course to flow into India. This “U” turn is due to?Syntaxial bending of geologically young Himalayas.

                                              Drainage System · The South Indian Rivers

                                              59 facts · 66 questions · 8 Must know

                                              Read the key facts and each question with its answer (30 min), then cover the answers and recall (10 min). Open the chapter in the full notes for explanations.
                                              Drainage System · The South Indian Rivers: key facts from the book
                                              • The main water divide in Peninsular India is formed by the Western Ghats, which run from north to south close to the western coast. Most of the major rivers of the Peninsula such as the Mahanadi, the Godavari, the Krishna, and the Cauvery flow eastwards and drain into the Bay of Bengal.
                                              • These rivers form deltas at their mouths. The Narmada, the Tapi and the Mahi are the major rivers that flow west and creats estuaries.
                                              • Peninsular rivers are characterized by a fixed course, absence of meanders and non-perennial flow of water. The Narmada and the Tapi river which flow through the rift valley are, however, exceptions.

                                              The South

                                              m (b) Indian Rivers

                                              • The Narmada: The Narmada originates from the Amarkantak Hill of the Maikal mountain range. It flows through a rift valley between the Satpura in the south and the Vindhyan range in the north. It forms Dhuandhar waterfall near Jabalpur. It travels a distance of 1312 km. It forms an estuary at its mouth. The Sardar Sarovar Dam has been constructed on this river.
                                              • The Tapi: The river Tapi originates from the Satpura range near Multai in the Betul district of Madhya Pradesh. It is 724 km long and flows through the states of Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat. It also forms an estuary at its mouth.
                                              • The Godavari: The Godavari is the longest river in Peninsular India. It is also known as the ‘Vriddha Ganga’ and ‘Dakshin Ganga’. It originates near Trimbakeshwar in the Nashik district of Maharashtra and discharges its water into the Bay of Bengal.
                                              • It is 1465 km long. Godavari basin extends over the states of Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Karnataka, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh and Union Territory of Puducherry. It forms the delta at its mouth. Its major tributaries are the Indravati, the Pranhita, the Manjra, etc.

                                              The Krishna: The Krishna river rises near the Mahabaleshwar in the Western Ghats. It is 1400 km long and discharges its water into the Bay of Bengal. Its major tributaries are the Koyna, the Tungabhadra and the Bhima, etc. Its basin covers the states of Maharashtra, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, and Telangana. Krishna river water dispute involves the states of Maharashtra, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh (Now- Andhra Pradesh and Telangana) since 1957. A number of committees and two different tribunals (KWDT-I & II) under the chairmanship ofretiredjudges of the Supreme Court, R.S. Bachawat (KWDT-I) and Brijesh Kumar (KWDT-II), have been constituted to adjudicate this dispute.

                                              • The Mahanadi: The Mahanadi rises near Sihawa (Dhamtari District) in Chhattisgarh and flows through Odisha to discharge its water into the Bay of Bengal. It forms a delta near Paradeep in the Bay of Bengal. It is 851 km long.
                                              • The Cauvery: The Cauvery river rises in the Brahmagiri hills (Talakaveri) of Kodagu district in Karnataka. It is 800 km long. It discharges its water into the Bay of Bengal near Poompuhar (Tamil Nadu). Its drainage basin covers the states of Kerala, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and the Union Territory of Puducherry. It forms the islands of Srirangam, Shivasamudram and Srirangapatna along its cource
                                              • Its major tributaries are Kabini, the Bhavani, the Amravati, the Hemavati, etc.
                                              • The largest waterfall in India in terms of volume is formed by the Cauvery river. It is known as the Shivasamudram.
                                              • An estuary is a partially enclosed coastal water body where freshwater from Rivers/streams mixes with salt water from the ocean. Estuaries form a transition zone between riverenvironments and maritime environments.
                                              • The world’s largest estuary is formed by the Saint Lawrence River.
                                              • Assertion (A): The rivers of Western Ghats do not form the delta.Both (A) and (R) are correct, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)

                                              A and R true, R explains A: Western Ghats' west-flowing rivers form no delta → short, fast courses over hard rocks; east-flowing rivers form deltas. Must know

                                              Full question and explanation · 3 paper(s)

                                              • Assertion (A): While all major rivers of peninsular India flow into the Bay of Bengal, the Narmada and the Tapi flow into the Arabian Sea.Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

                                              A and R true, R explains A: Narmada and Tapi flow west to the Arabian Sea as they run in rift valleys; other major peninsular rivers → Bay of Bengal. Must know

                                              Full question and explanation · 2 paper(s)

                                              • The Narmada river flows to the West, while most other large peninsular rivers flow to the East. why?—

                                              Narmada flows west because it occupies a linear rift valley between the Vindhyas and Satpuras; rises near Amarkantak (Maikal range), MP. Must know

                                              Full question and explanation · 3 paper(s)

                                              • Assertion (A): The Narmada forms a delta at its mouth.(A) is false, but (R) is true

                                              A false, R true: Narmada forms no delta because it flows through a rift valley (fault trough) and deposits no silt. Must know

                                              Full question and explanation · 5 paper(s)

                                              • Which one of the following rivers is different from the others?Narmada

                                              Odd one → Narmada flows west to the Arabian Sea (rift valley between Satpura and Vindhya); Tungabhadra, Penganga, Mahanadi drain to the Bay of Bengal.

                                              • Which of the following characteristic feature is appropriate for Narmada river?Structural origin

                                              Narmada → structural origin: it flows along a fault.

                                              • Which of the following rivers does not make delta?—

                                              Narmada and Tapi (west-flowing, rift valleys, fast flow, little silt) → form estuaries, not deltas; Tapi does not fall into the Bay of Bengal. Must know

                                              Cauvery → forms islands of Srirangapatnam, Sivasamudram, Srirangam; rises in Brahmagiri hills (Talakaveri, Kodagu, Karnataka); flows through Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu. Must know
