                                                    Drainage System · Other Rivers: key facts from the book
                                                    • The Sutlej originates from the Rakas Lake near Kailash Mountain and Mansarovar Lake in Tibet. Flowing in a north west direction it enters Himachal Pradesh near Shipki La Pass. It forms deep gorge by eroding Himalayan ranges in Himachal region. It has a length of approx. 1500 km, and the Beas river meets Sutlej near Harike in Punjab.
                                                    • The Son river originates near Amarkantak Hills in Anuppur district (M.P.)/Gaurela- Pendra-Marwahi district (Chhattisgarh). It meets river Ganga near Patna (Bihar). Its important tributaries are Johilla, Mahanadi, Banas, Gopad, Rihand, Ghogher, Kanhar and North Koel.
                                                    • The Kosi river is formed by the confluence of three streams namely the sun Kosi, the Arun Kosi and the Tamur Kosi, all taking their origin in the Himalayan region of Nepal and Tibet. It has a length of 720 km and meets Ganga river at Kursela, Katihar (Bihar). It has seven tributaries, of which Arun is the most important.
                                                    • The Kosi is known for its disastrous floods and especially for maximum shifting of its courses. That’s why it is also called as the ‘Sorrow of Bihar’.
                                                    • Damodar river is known as the ‘Sorrow of Bengal’: It originates from Khamarpat Hill in the Chota Nagpur Plateau region and flows through a rift valley.
                                                    • It has a number of tributaries, such as Barakar, Konar, and Jamunia. Its total length is 541 km. It carries the water of Rupnarayan river and flows into the Hugli 48 km south of Kolkata.
                                                    • Eden canal was taken out from Damodar river. The 300 km of the river between Giridih and Durgapur has become a Biological Desert.
                                                    • The Hagari River originates in the Western Ghats Flowing through Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh, it merges with the Tungabhadra River. It is also known by the name of Vedavathi river. The River Veda and the River Avathi originate with Sahyadri and meet each other in Pura to become Vedavathi.
                                                    • The Jhelum River rises from a spring at Verinag situated at the foot of Pir Panjal in the Valley of Kashmir.
                                                    • It flows through Srinagar and the Wular Lake before entering Pakistan through a deep narrow gorge.
                                                    • The Jhelum and Ravi riversjoin the Chenab river in Pakistan at different points, Jhelum near Trimmu, Ravi South of Ahmadpur Sial.
                                                    • The Kishan Ganga river is a tributary of the Jhelum, which is known as Neelum in Pakistan. The Luni river originates in the south-west of Ajmer in Aravalli Range, where it is known as Sagarmati. It passes through the southeastern portion of the Thar Desert and ends in the marshy lands of Rann of Kutch in Gujarat, after traveling a distance of511 km. The Shyok River is known as ‘River of Death’ in the Karakoram region. Ancient evidence indicates that it was also a medium of trade between Yarkand in Central Asia and Ladakh.
                                                    • The Zanskar river flows through hard rock and forms deep gorges in Zanskar (Zaskar) range. It originates on the border of Himachal Pradesh and Ladakh (U.T.) near Sarchu a high latitudinal plateau part. It flows North and then towards the east joining the Indus at Nimu. Its length is 150 km.
                                                    • The Spiti river originates from Kunzam La. It merges into the Sutlej river near Namgia at Khab in Kinnaur district of Himachal Pradesh.
                                                    • The Kali river rises near Diggi village in Uttara Kannada district of Karnataka. It follows an arch-shaped course in a West-ward direction and flows into the Arabian sea.
                                                    • The Sankosh river originates in northern Bhutan and flows into Brahmaputra river near the border of Assam and West Bengal. It forms the boundary between Assam and West Bengal. In Bhutan, it is known as Puna Tsang Chu.
                                                    • The Mahi river originates in M.P. and enters Rajasthan in the district of Banswara, then flows in a south-west direction of Gujarat and falls into the Gulf of Khambat.
                                                    • The Mithi river originates from Vihar Lake in Mumbai. After flowing 2 km, the water from Powai Lake also merges in this stream. It travels a distance of 18 km and falls into the Arabian Sea near the Bay of Mahim.
                                                    • The Tel river is an important tributary of Mahanadi river.
                                                    • The Kapili (Kopili) river is an important tributary of Brahmaputra.
                                                    • Compare the Himalayan river with the Peninsular river based on the following comparisons:1 and 2 only

                                                    True: Himalayan rivers mostly perennial (glacier-fed), Peninsular mostly rain-fed; Himalayan gradient steeper. False: Peninsular rivers erode more (Himalayan rivers do).

                                                          Drainage System · Cities Located on the Bank of Rivers: key facts from the book
                                                          • The rivers have always played a vital role in economic development of India. They are the sources of livelihood for humans from ancient times. In India, there are many cities located on the banks of rivers. Bhagirathi, a major tributary of Ganga, originates from Gomukh in Uttarkashi district of Uttarakhand. Uttarkashi is located on the bank of river Bhagirathi. The cities of Haridwar, Fatehpur, Kanpur, Varanasi, Bhagalpur, Patna, etc. are the important cities located on the bank of river Ganga. Prayagraj is located at the confluence of rivers Ganga and Yamuna.
                                                          • Delhi, Agra, Mathura, Etawah, etc. are the important cities located on the banks of the river Yamuna.
                                                          • Ludhiana and Firozpur (Punjab) are located on the old bank of river Sutlej. Presently, Sutlej river flows 13 km north of these cities.
                                                          • Hyderabad is located on the bank of the river Musi or Musinuru (a tributary of the river Krishna). The famous city of Vijayawada of Andhra Pradesh is located on the bank of the river Krishna. Nanded, Nashik (Maharashtra) and Rajamahendravaram (Andhra Pradesh) are located on the bank of river Godavari.
                                                          • In the Union Territory of Jammu & Kashmir, Srinagar is located on the bank of river Jhelum and in the UT of Ladakh, Leh is located on the right bank of river Indus.
                                                          • Ahmedabad is located on the bank of river Sabarmati.
                                                          • Lucknow, the capital of Uttar Pradesh, is located on the bank of the river Gomati.
                                                          • Surat (Gujarat) is located on the bank of river Tapti or Tapi.
                                                          • Jamshedpur (Industrial city of Jharkhand) is located on the bank of river the Subarnarekha and Kharkai.
                                                          • Jagdalpur (Chhattisgarh) is located on the bank of river Indravati.
                                                          • Jabalpur (M.P.) is located on the bank of river Narmada. Ujjain (M.P.) is located on the bank of river Kshipra. The ancient name of this city was Ujjayini (capital of Mahajanapada of North Avanti). The city is also known as Mahakal Nagari.
                                                          • Bareilly (U.P) is located on the bank of river Ram Ganga. Gaurikund, Rambara, and Guptakashi (Uttarakhand) are located on the bank of river Mandakini and Govindghat is located on the bank of river Alaknanda and Laxman Ganga.
                                                          • Ayodhya is located on the bank of river Saryu.
                                                          • Gorakhpur (U.P.) is located on the bank of river Rapti.
                                                          • Guwahati and Dibrugarh (Assam) are located on the bank of river Brahmaputra. The city of Kota (Rajasthan) is located on the bank of river Chambal.
                                                          Drainage System · Waterfalls and Lakes: key facts from the book
                                                          • A waterfall generally refers to a vertical or steep fall of a water body. The origin of waterfalls may be natural as well as artificial.
                                                          • Natural waterfalls are often found in the mountainous regions because the land there is full of ups and downs. Most of the waterfalls in India are found in the southern region. According to World Waterfall Database, the Jog is the largest waterfall in India in terms of width. It is created by Sharavathi river in Karnataka. Shivasamudram, created by Cauvery river, is the largest fall in terms of volume.
                                                          • Hundru waterfall is created by Subarnarekha river (45 km from Ranchi). Its height is 98m.
                                                          • Kapil-Dhara waterfall is formed by Narmada river in Anuppur district (M.P.).

                                                          According to the World Waterfall Database, the height of Kunchikal waterfall is approx. 183 m. On this basis, it is no longer the highest waterfall in India. The height of Barehipani waterfall, as per the new database is 217 metres. According to the Meghalaya Institute of Governance the height of Nohkalikai waterfall 340 metres. So as per the new database, Nohkalikai is the tallest plunge waterfall. The rapid erosion of soft rocks as compared to the hard rocks leads to the creation of waterfalls.

                                                          Lakes-

                                                          • Vembanad lake is the largest lagoon lake in Kerala. Chilika lagoon is a saline water lake at the end of Mahanadi. Nakki lake is located in Mount Abu, Rajasthan.
                                                          • Roopkund lake is known as Mysterious lake. It is a glacial lake in Uttarakhand. The lake has been in limelight because of the human skeletons found here. The Gomti river originates from Phulhar lake, which is found near Madhotanda (Pilibhit).
                                                          • Ashtamudi lake is a lagoon in Kollam district of Kerala. Ashtamudi means eight branches. It is an important wetland according to Ramsar Convention. In Assam, Chandubi Lake, Deepor Beel (Lake), and Haflong Lakes are important lakes. Chembarambakkam lake is situated in Tamil Nadu (South of Chennai). It is the source of the Adyar river. The Chennai city meets its demand for water supply from this lake. There are two lakes Hussain Sagar and Osman Sagar (Artificial) in Hyderabad.
                                                          • Renuka Lake and Nako Lake are located in Himachal Pradesh. Kolleru is a freshwater lake located in Andhra Pradesh. Pushkar Lake is an artificial lake located in Ajmer district of Rajasthan. India’s largest inland saline water lake is Sambhar located in Rajasthan. Pulicat is the second largest brackish water lake in India after Chilika Lake.
                                                          • Sriharikota Island separates Pulicat Lake from the Bay of Bengal.

                                                          Ramsar Convention (1971)

                                                          • The Ramsar Convention on Wetlands of International Importance is an international treaty for the conservation and sustainable use ofwetlands. It was adopted in the Iranian city of Ramsar in 1971 and came into force in 1975. It is the only global environmental treaty that deals with a particular ecosystem.

                                                          Lagoons are shallow coastal bodies of water near a sea or an ocean, separated by a series of barrier islands that lie parallel to shorelines.

                                                          • Wular lake is the largest freshwater lake of India located in Jammu and Kashmir (U.T.). Dal lake is located in Srinagar (Zabarwan Range). Periyar lake is located in Kerala. Loktak lake is a freshwater lake in Manipur. Keibul Lamjao National Park is located in the south western part of Loktak Lake.

                                                                Climate: key facts from the book

                                                                i. Monsoon

                                                                • The word ‘Monsoon’ is derived from the Arabic word ‘Mausim’ which means season.
                                                                • Traditionally, the term "Monsoon" refers to the seasonal reversal in wind patterns that brings rainfall, producing distinct wet and dry seasons in many tropical and subtropical regions, especially in South and Southeast Asia but not limited to them. India receives near-about 75% of its total precipitation from the southwest monsoon. The monsoon is active from June to September, which is very important for agriculture in India. The southwest monsoon normally arrives of the Kerala coast (the southern tip of the Indian Peninsula) around the first week of June, though the exact date varies from year to year and may be slightly earlier or later.

                                                                Origin of Indian Monsoon

                                                                • Monsoon is a result of differential rates of heating and cooling of land and sea. The sun is vertical over the Tropic of Cancer in summer season, and the northern regions of the Indian landmass get heated. This leads to the formation of low pressure conditions over the Indian subcontinent. On the other hand, the Indian Ocean is colder, so high pressure is generated, leading to northward shifting of Inter Tropical Convergence Zone.
                                                                • The Inter Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) is a low-pressure belt near the equator where trade winds of the northern and the southern hemispheres converge.
                                                                • Due to the northward shift of the ITCZ, the trade winds of the southern hemisphere cross the equator between 40° and 60° E longitudes and starts blowing from the southwest to the northeast under the influence of the Coriolis force. It becomes southwest monsoon.
                                                                • In winter, the ITCZ moves southward, and so the reversal of winds from northeast to south and southwest takes place. They are called northeast monsoons.
                                                                • The sudden onset of the moisture-laden winds associated with violent thunder and lightning is often termed as the ‘burst’ of the monsoon. The monsoon may burst in the first week of June in the coastal area of Kerala.
                                                                • The monsoon approaches the Indian landmass in two main branches:

                                                                (i) The Arabian Sea branch

                                                                (ii) The Bay of Bengal branch

                                                                • The Tibetan Plateau has a very broad impact on the Indian climatic pattern.
                                                                • Rainfall received from the southwest monsoon winds is seasonal in character, occurring between June and September. Monsoonal rainfall is largely governed by relief or topography. The monsoon rainfall has a declining trend with increasing distance from the sea. The rainless intervals are known as ‘breaks’ in the monsoon.

                                                                The Retreat of the Monsoon - The months of October and November are known for retreating monsoons.

                                                                • The weather in the retreating monsoon is dry in north India whereas it is associated with rain in the eastern part of the Peninsula. The widespread rainfall during this season is associated with the movement of cyclonic depressions that develop in situ over the south-east Bay of Bengal and the adjoining Anddman sea and then cross the eastern coast of the Southern Peninsula. These tropical cyclones are very destructive. A bulk of the rainfall on the Coromandel coast is derived from these depressions and cyclones. Such cyclonic storms are less frequent in the Arabian Sea.

                                                                • El-Nino is a complex weather system bringing drought, floods and other weather extremes in different parts of the world. It occurs with the sudden appearance of warm currents off the coast of Peru (warm equatorial current replaces cold Peruvian current).
                                                                Climate · Rainfall: key facts from the book
                                                                • Generally in India rainfall occurs from the month of June to September when south-west monsoon is effective throughout the country. In this period, the low-pressure zone of North Western India is very intense and systematic. Due to low air pressure, south-east winds from the tropic of Capricorn in the Southern Hemisphere cross the equator and are attracted towards the Indian Peninsula. Passing over the oceans these winds are filled with humidity and split into two branches - Arabian Sea branch and Bay of Bengal branch.
                                                                • When the south-west monsoon winds enter the terrestrial area, it rains with an intense thundering and torrential storms. The arrival of these winds and rainfall is called ‘burst’ of the monsoon.
                                                                • The speed of these winds is about 30 km/hon average and they become effective throughout the country within a month.
                                                                • According to the data Rainfall Statistics of India (2024), almost the entire rainfall is received from the southwest monsoon (June-September).
                                                                • Monsoon winds of the Arabian Sea are obstructed by the Western Ghats. These winds climb the slope of the Western Ghats and soon become cool causing heavy rainfall on the windward side of Western Ghats. These winds cause little rainfall to the east of the Western Ghats. The region of low rainfall is known as the rain-shadow area.

                                                                R

                                                                • Another branch of monsoon winds from the Arabian Sea causes rainfall in the extensive areas of central India. Thereafter, they enter the Ganga plains and mingle with the Bay of Bengal branch. The Bay of Bengal branch of monsoon winds causes rainfall in northeast and Gangetic plains reaching as far as the Punjab plains.
                                                                • The actual annual rainfall in India is about 1206.6 mm (Data - 2024) but it has great spatial variations. The highest amount of rainfall occurs along the west coast of the Western Ghats as well as in the Eastern-Himalayan region and Meghalaya.
                                                                • Mawsynram receives the highest average annual rainfall in the world. According to the data Rainfall Statistics of India 2024, annually, the District of East Khasi Hills in Meghalaya received the highest rainfall of 6171.0mm whereas the District of Leh in Ladakh (UT) received the lowest rainfall of 56.967mm, which resembles with the normal pattern of rainfall in India.
                                                                • Mango showers are pre-monsoon showers in Kerala and Karnataka. They are known as such because they help in the early ripening of the mangoes.
                                                                Climate · Winter Rainfall: key facts from the book
                                                                • The winter (northeasterly) winds are generally dry over most of India, but after crossing the Bay of Bengal they pick up moisture and cause rainfall over the south-eastern coast of India during the northeast (retreating) monsoon season. Most parts of India do not receive much rainfall in the winter season. Some weak temperate cyclones from the Mediterranean Sea cause rainfall in Punjab, Haryana, Delhi and Western Uttar Pradesh. Although the amount is meager, it is highly beneficial for Rabi crops. Central India, northern parts of the Southern Peninsula, Arunachal Pradesh and Assam also receive winter rainfall.
                                                                • During October to December, the northeast (retreating) monsoon winds, after crossing the Bay of Bengal, pick up moisture and cause heavy to torrential rainfall over the Tamil Nadu coast (Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Karaikal), Southern Andhra Pradesh (Costal andhra Pradesh, Yanam and Rayalaseema), South- interior Karnataka and parts of southern Kerala (including Mahe).

                                                                      Natural Disasters: key facts from the book

                                                                      Natural disasters are catastrophic events of atmospheric, geological and hydrological origin that can cause fatalities, property damage and socio-environmental disruption.

                                                                      • Volcanic eruptions, Earthquakes, Oceanic Vibrations, Droughts, Floods, Cyclones, Soil erosion, Snow avalanches, Mud Flows, etc. are example of Natural Disasters. Among these most of the disasters are produced by Natural forces. However, unwanted activities of human’s increase the intensity of these disasters. Due to the exploitative activities of human beings, the adverse effects of these disasters have increased.
                                                                      • The Himalayan Mountain is a new fold mountain whose growth is still continuing. The collision of the Indian Plate along the boundary of Nepal formed the orogenic belt that created the Himalayan Mountains. The Indian Plate is moving faster than the Eurasian Plate in a northward direction. Hence, the associated compression due to this phenomenon has kept the Himalayas growing in size.
                                                                      • The Southern Plateau is relatively more stable, yet the rare events of low intensity earthquakes in the region raise questions about the stability of Peninsular India.
                                                                      • On the basis of data provided by the India Meteorological Department and other agencies, the Bureau of Indian Standards has published the latest version of seismic zone map of India. The Bureau of Indian standards has prepared ‘Earthquake Resistant Design Code of India, IS - 1893, Part I: 2002 which is a new edition of seismic zone mapping of India. In this, India has been divided into four seismic zones on the basis of earthquake intensity - namely Zone II, Zone III, Zone IV and Zone V. Each zone indicates the effects of an earthquake at a particular place based on the observations of the affected area and can also be described using a descriptive scale like the Modified Mercalli Intensity Scale or the Medvedev-Sponhever-Karnik Scale (MSK).
                                                                      Seismic ZoneIntensity
                                                                      Zone II (Low Intensity)MSKVI or less, Low Damage

                                                                      Risk Zone

                                                                      Zone III (Moderate Intensity) MSK VII, Moderate Damage Risk Zone

                                                                      Zone IV (High Intensity) MSK VIII, High Damage Risk Zone

                                                                      Zone V (Very High Intensity) MSK IX or greater, Very High Damage Risk Zone

                                                                      • Zone V: Zone V covers 10.9% of the area of the country with the highest risk zone that suffers earthquakes of intensity MSK IX or greater. The IS code assigns a zone factor of 0.36 for Zone V. It is referred to as the very high damage risk zone. The region of J&K (UT), Ladakh (UT) some parts of Uttarakhand and Bihar, the North - East Indian region and the Rann of Kutch, Andaman & Nicobar etc., fall in this zone.
                                                                      • Zone IV - The IS code assigns a zone factor of 0.24 for Zone IV. The Indo - Gangetic basin and the National Capital Territory of Delhi, as well as the rest of Himalayas, are included. in Zone IV. In Maharashtra, the Patan area (Koyananagar) falls under Zone IV.

                                                                      This zone covers the northern parts of Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and West Bengal, parts of Gujarat and small portions of Maharashtra near the west coast and Rajasthan. It covers almost 17.3% of the areas of the country.

                                                                      • Zone III - The IS code assigns a zone factor of 0.16 for Zone III. It covers the the Lakshadweep Islands. This zone is classified as a moderate damage risk zone. It covers 30.4% of the areas of the country.
                                                                      • Zone II- The IS code assigns zone factor of 0.10 for Zone II. Zone II is determined by combining the previous Zone I and Zone II. It covers 41.4% of India. Major parts of the peninsular region and Karnataka Plateau fall in this zone. Thus, it does not come under the zone of high seismic intensity.
                                                                      • Tsunami is a Japanese word, which consists of two words, ‘tsu’ meaning ‘harbours’ and ‘nami’ meaning ‘wave’. According to the High Powered Committee on Disaster Management Report (2001) of India, it originates from events like Earthquakes in the Ocean, Landslides, Volcanic explosions, etc. The majority of Tsunamis originate from earthquakes that occur on the ocean floor. Tsunami is also called the ‘Harbour waves’ or ‘Sea waves’. The Indian Tsunami Early Warning System (ITEWS) is established at Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Science (INCOIS), Hyderabad. It started operating in October 2007. On 26th December, 2004, a Tsunami, that originated from the Indian Ocean, hit the Coromandel coast of India. The Coromandel coast is southeastern coast of the Indian subcontinent. The coastlines run from False Divi Point in north to Kanyakumari in the south.
                                                                      • The India Meteorological Department was constituted in 1875 under the Ministry of Earth Sciences, with its headquarters at New Delhi.
                                                                      • The Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology and the deputy director's office of IMD (India Meteorological Department) are situated in Pune. Kolkata was the first head office of India Meteorological Department. The headquarters of IMD was later shifted to Shimla in 1905, then to Pune in 1928, and finally to Delhi in 1944.
                                                                      • Floods are an overflow of water submerging land is usually dry. The second important consequence of uncertainty and irregularity of monsoons is the flooding.
                                                                      • “The Flood Forecast & Warning Organisation” was set up by Central Water Commission in 1969 to establish forecasting sites on Inter-State rivers in various flood prone areas of the country.
                                                                      • The ‘National Flood Forecasting and Warning Network’ of Central Water Commission, comprises of 338 flood forecasting sites.
                                                                      • The flood region of Uttar Pradesh is divided into high flood prone and low flood prone regions.
                                                                      • A cyclone is a large scale air mass that rotates around a strong centre of low pressure. They are usually characterized by spiraling winds that rotate anti-clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern hemisphere. Tropical cyclones are characterized by large pressure gradients.
                                                                      • The centre of the cyclone is mostly a warm, low-pressure, cloudless core known as the eye of the storm. Generally, the isobars are closely placed to each other, showing high-pressure gradients.

                                                                      Under the influence of gravity, a landslide is an activity involving the sliding of rocks and soil along slopes.

                                                                      • The frequency of landslides has been increasing in the Himalayas. Its root causes are increased frequency of earthquakes as well as man-made activities such as the construction of roads and dams. Large scale mining has been conducted for the construction of roads, dams, and minerals in the Himalayas in recent years. That is why the frequency of landslides has increased in the Himalayas.
                                                                      • The first Disaster Management Training Institute in country has been established in Latur, Maharashtra.
                                                                      Soils · Black Soil: key facts from the book
                                                                      • The Black soil is also known as the ‘Regur Soil’, or the ‘Black Cotton Soil’, ‘Tropical Black Earth’ or the ‘Tropical Chernozem’.
                                                                      • These soils are formed by the weathering and erosional work of Basalt Lava.
                                                                      • These soils cover most of the Deccan trap especially in the states of Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Telangana. Geographically, it spreads over
                                                                      • 5.46 Lakh sq km in different Indian states.
                                                                      • The Black soils are very suitable for cultivation of cotton. These soils are rich in Lime, Iron, Magnesium corbonate, Alumina, Potash and Calcium. They also contain Potash but they lack in Phosphorus, Nitrogen and Organic Matter.
                                                                      • The black soils are generally clayey, deep, and impermeable. They swell and become sticky when wet and shrink when dried. During the dry season, these soils develop wide cracks. Thus, there occurs a kind of self ploughing. Because of this characteristic of slow absorption and loss of moisture, the black soil retains the moisture for a long time.
                                                                      • The colour of Black Cotton soil ranges from deep black, similer to the colour of Chestnut.
                                                                      • According to ‘Krebs’, the Black soil is a mature soil in which special reliefand climate play an important role.
                                                                      Soils · Laterite Soil: key facts from the book
                                                                      • F.Buchanan- Hamilton carried out research on Laterite soil for the first time in 1807. Its name has been derived from the Latin word ‘Later’ which means ‘brick’.
                                                                      • These soils are as soft as butter when wet but become harder like bricks when dry.
                                                                      • The laterite soil is formed under conditions of high temperature and heavy rainfall with alternate wet and dry periods, which leads to the leaching of soil, leaving only oxides of iron and aluminium. The humus content of the soil is removed quickly by bacteria that thrive well in high temperatures.
                                                                      • These soils are poor in Organic Matter, Nitrogen, Phosphate, and Calcium while Iron Oxide, Aluminium Oxides and Potash are in excess. Hence, laterites are not suitable for cultivation. However, the application of manures and fertilizers is required to make the soils fertile for cultivation.
                                                                      • They are well developed in parts of Western Ghats, Eastern Ghats, South Maharashtra, parts of Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, West Bengal, Kerala, Jharkhand, Meghalaya, and Assam. Laterite soil is widely spread in India and covers an area of 2.48 lakh sq. km. It is mostly found in Kerala (Malabar Coastal region) followed by Maharashtra. In laterite soil a common relationship is found between height and chemical composition. The upper parts are more acidic than the inner ones.
                                                                      Soils · Alluvial Soil: key facts from the book
                                                                      • Alluvial soils are widespread in the northern plains and the river valleys. These soils cover about 15 lakh sq. km or about 45.6% of the total area of the country.
                                                                      • The alluvial soil is largely found in the Indo-Gangetic plain starting from Punjab in the west to the West Bengal and Assam in the east. These soils are also found in deltas of Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Cauvery, where they are called deltaic Alluvium. Alluvial soils are formed mainly by Himalayan sediments and sea retreats.
                                                                      • The colour of Alluvial soil varies from light grey to ash grey. They vary in nature from Sandy, Loam to Clay.
                                                                      • Generally they are rich in Phosphoric Acid, Potash, Lime, and Organic Matter but poor in Nitrogen and Humus content.
                                                                      • Due to the cultivation of leguminous crops nitrogen fixation takes place at a faster rate in these soils. They are suitable for irrigation which helps in growing crops like Wheat, Rice, Sugarcane, Jute, Cotton, Maize, Oilseed, Fruits and Vegetables.
                                                                      • Generally loamy soil has 40% sand particles, 18% clay particles and 42% silt particles.
                                                                      • Types of Alluvial Soil:

                                                                      Khadar - Khadar is the new alluvium and is deposited by floods annually enriching the soil by depositing fine silts. It always remains fertile.

                                                                      Bangar - Bangar represents a system of older alluvium deposited away from the flood plains. Its color is pale reddish brown and in this, nodules are formed at large scale.

                                                                      Bhabar - Bhabar is the gently sloping coarse alluvial zone below the Shiwalik Hills, where streams disappear into permeable sediments.

                                                                      Tarai - The marshy lowland region south of the Bhabar is called Tarai (Terai). The soil of this region is generally rich in nitrogen and organic matter but poor in phosphate. The ancient alluvial soil found at higher altitudes in this region is known as Rarh Plain.

                                                                            Soils · Soils : Miscellaneous: key facts from the book
                                                                            • Red Soil - Red Soil in India, is formed by weathering of ancient crystalline igneous and metamorphic rocks.
                                                                            • The higher concentration of iron is responsible for the red colour of the soil.
                                                                            • These soils are found in regions of low rainfall and are obviously more leached than Laterite soils. The red soils cover a large portion of land in India (approximately 3.5 lakh sq. km).
                                                                            • Red soils are poor in Phosphorus, Nitrogen and Lime content. They are found in the Indian States of Western Tamil Nadu, Southern Karnataka, Southern Maharashtra, north-eastern Andhra Pradesh and some parts of M.P., Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Telangana and Chotanagpur (Jharkhand). The soil develops a reddish colour due to a wide diffusion of iron in crystalline and metamorphic rocks. It appears yellow when it occurs in a hydrated form. Desert Soil - The Desert soil covers an area of approx. 1.42 lakh sq. km. The rainfall in these areas ranges from less than 50 cm. The temperature is very high. The avg. temperature of soil is 35°C. These soils are formed in dry climatic condition. They are found in Rajasthan, Saurashtra (Gujarat), Kutch, Southern Punjab. They contain a low amount of organic matter and nitrogen.
                                                                            • Legume crops enrich the soils with nitrogen content by atmospheric nitrogen fixation. Plants contributing to nitrogen fixation include Soybeans, alfalfa, Lupins, Peanuts and Pulses.
                                                                            Soils · Acidic and Alkali Soil: key facts from the book
                                                                            • The soil pH is a measure of the acidity or alkalinity in the soil- pH below 7 is acidic and above 7 is alkaline. Generally, the pH value of crop soil is 6.0-7.0.
                                                                            • Acidic soil is sedimentary in nature. It has mixed laterite, ferrous red and another red soil group.
                                                                            • These soils are formed by the humid climate, acidic material and geomorphology. Due to temperature, humid climate and heavy rain, rapid erosion occurs in soil and increases the rate of leaching of bases. Due to high temperature with heavy rainfalll, and leaching, acidic soil is formed.
                                                                            • Factors causing acidity in the soil include leaching (due to heavy rainfall), acidic substances, acid-forming fertilizers and soluble salts, etc.

                                                                            Alkali Soil –

                                                                            • Generally, the alkaline soil is found in India in dry and wetland regions. It is fromed due to capillary action ofcations such as Mg⁺², Na⁺, Ca⁺⁺, which are deposited on the surface of the soil. This type of soil is mainly distributed in South Punjab, Southern Haryana and West-Rajasthan.
                                                                            • Gypsum (CaSO₄) is used to change the alkalinity of the soil and remove the salinity from it.
                                                                            Soils · Soil Erosion and Conservation: key facts from the book
                                                                            • Soil Erosion - The destruction of the soil cover is described as soil erosion. Soil erosion refers to the wearing away and removal of the topsoil by natural physical forces such as water, wind and air.
                                                                            • Topsoil is the top layer of soil and is the most fertile because it contains the most organic, nutrient-rich substances.

                                                                            Causes of Soil Erosion-

                                                                            (1) Deforestation

                                                                            (2) Disturbance in the natural drainage pattern, improper design of waterways.

                                                                            (3) Grazing, Water, Wind, Air

                                                                            (4) Poor vegetation and cultivation

                                                                            • The most affected regions by soil erosion in India are Badlands of the Chambal and Yamuna rivers, Western Himalaya (Shivalik region), Chota Nagpur plateau, Malwa plateau, Black Soil region of Maharashtra, arid regions of Haryana, Rajasthan and Gujarat. Ravines of Chambal valley are formed by Gully erosion.
                                                                            • Splash Erosion: The erosion due to the impact of falling raindrops on soil-surface leading to the destruction of the crumb structure is known as the raindrop or splash erosion. This is the first stage of erosion.
                                                                            • Sheet Erosion: Sometimes water flows as a sheet over large areas down a slope. In such cases, the topsoil is washed away. This is known as sheet erosion. It is the second stage of soil erosion.
                                                                            • Rill Erosion :- This is the third stage of sheet erosion. If erosion continues unchecked for a sufficient time then rills or small finger-shaped grooves which are a few centimetres in depth may develop on the landscape. Over a period of time, the fine rills increase in number and also become deeper and wider, resembling the twigs, branches and trunk of a tree. This is called rill erosion.
                                                                            • Gully Erosion :- This is the fourth stage of erosion. With further erosion of the soil, the rills may become deeper and enlarge the (region between the Tapti and Sabarmati valleys, and are ultimately turning into gullies. Gully erosion is also responsible for the formation of ravines.
                                                                            • Stream Channel Erosion :- Water flowing through a channel corrodes its banks and base until a stable base is formed. This form of erosion is known as stream channel erosion.
                                                                            • Soil Conservation :- Prevention of soil erosion is also called conservation of soil. The soil erosion can be prevented by promoting afforestation, Crop Rotation, Terrace Farming, Building Dams, Shelter Belts, Ebankments, etc.
                                                                            • Crop rotation refers to the practice of growing different types of crops over the same area in different seasons. It enriches soil fertility and helps in pest control. Plants keep soil bound in locks of roots, and thus, prevent soil erosion.
                                                                            • Reduced or zero tillage of the land in farming is a way of growing crops or pasture year after year without disturbing the soil through tillage. It helps in soil moisture conservation.
                                                                            Natural Vegetation: key facts from the book
                                                                            • Natural Vegetation refers to the flora that grows naturally without human aid and they change their physical stability, shape and size with respect to the environment.
                                                                            • The Type of vegetation found in an area depends on the geographical factors such as humidity, temperature, soil, rainfall, altitude, etc. On this basis, there are several types of vegetation found in India.

                                                                            1. Tropical Evergreen Forest-

                                                                            • The tropical evergreen and semi-evergreen forest is usually found in warm and humid areas receiving more than 200 cm of rainfall and a mean annual temperature above 22° C. The relative humidity of this region is more than 70%.
                                                                            • Due to high humidity and temperature, trees are very tall and intensive (dense). They are also called as “Selvas”.
                                                                            • There is a different time for leaf fall for different species of trees, due to which the entire forest is evergreen. The tropical evergreen forest in India is found in Assam, Kerala, West Bengal, The Andaman-Nicobar Islands, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram and Western coastal plain.

                                                                            The major species found in the tropical evergreen forest include Cinchona, Rubber, Coconut, Bamboo, Mahogany, Ebony, etc.

                                                                            • 2. Tropical Deciduous or Monsoon Forests:
                                                                            • Tropical deciduous forests are also called monsoon forests. Trees shed their leaves in the dry season to conserve water. The average rainfall in this region is 70-200 cm. On the basis of availability of water, these forests can be categorized as Tropical Moist Deciduous Forest and Tropical Dry Deciduous Forest. In India, Tropical Moist Deciduous Forests are found in the eastern slope of the Western Ghats, the northeastern region of the Indian peninsula and the Bhabar and Tarai (Terai) region.
                                                                            • Trees found in these forests include Sal, Teak, Neem, Shisham and Mango. Hardwood trees are extremely helpful for making furniture.

                                                                            3. Tropical Dry Deciduous Forest:

                                                                            • These forests are found in the region where there is annual rainfall ranging between 70 and 100 cm. These forests are found mainly in Uttar Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.
                                                                            • The main trees are Rosewood, Mango, Sandalwood, and Mahua. These forests are economically important and valuable.

                                                                            4. Arid Forest:

                                                                            • Arid forests are also referred to as ‘Tropical Thorn Forests’. They are found in the areas receiving less than 70 cm rainfall.
                                                                            • They include semi-arid areas of south-west Punjab, South-west Haryana, Rajasthan and Gujarat.
                                                                            • These forests consist of a variety of grasses and shrubs. In these forests, plants remain leafless for most of the year. Important species found are babool, ber, wild date palm, khair, neem, khejri, palas, etc.

                                                                            5. Delta Forest :-

                                                                            • Deltaic forest is also known as mangrove, swampy or littoral forest. Mangroves grow along the coast in the salt marshes, tidal creeks, mudflats and estuaries. Deltaic forest develops in the deltaic regions of the Ganga, Godavari, Brahmaputra, Krishna rivers, etc. The Sundarban forest is the best example of a deltaic forests.

                                                                            6. Montane Forests:-

                                                                            In mountainous areas, the decrease in temperature with increasing altitude leads to a corresponding change in natural vegetation. Mountain forests can be classified into two types: the northern mountain forest and the southern mountain forest.

                                                                            • The Himalayan range shows a succession of vegetation from tropical to tundra.

                                                                            Deciduous types of forests are found in the foothills of the Himalayas. It is succeeded by the wet temperat type of forests between an altitude of about 1000-2000m. Evergreen broad leaftrees such as oak and chest nut are predominantly found here. At about 2000-3000m altitude on the southern slopes of the Himalayas, temperate forests containing coniferous trees like Pine, Deodar, Silver Fir, Spruce and Cedar are found. These forests are also found in places with high altitudes in southern and north-east India.

                                                                            • Alpine forests grow all along the Himalayas at altitudes ranging between about 3000-4900 meters. Deodar, a highly valued endemic species grows mainly in the western part of the Himalayan range at an altitude of about 1500-3000 meter.
                                                                            • The southern mountain forests include the forests found in three distinct areas of the peninsula e.g. the Western Ghats, the Vindhyas and the Nilgiris. Vegetation in these forests is temperate in higher regions and sub tropical in lower regions. The temperate forests are called sholas in the Nilgiris, Ana malai and Palani Hills.
                                                                            • Butea monosperma is called the "flame of the forest". It is also known as Dhak or Palash. Palash has been declared as the state flower of Uttar Pradesh.

                                                                                  Irrigation and Canals: key facts from the book
                                                                                  • India is situated in tropical, sub-tropical and temperate climate area. The maximum area of the country comes under a high-temperature zone, except for the western Himalayas, north-eastern-Assam, Meghalaya and some parts of South India.
                                                                                  • High evaporation occurs due to high temperatures. Therefore, there is a need for irrigation to fulfill the deficit of moisture in sown crops.
                                                                                  • As per Land Use Statistics for 2022- 23, the net irrigated area during 2022-23 was 79312 thousand hectares, out of which 22.85% was accounted by canal source of irrigation, 2.82% by tanks, 49.34% by Tube wells, 13.46% by other well and remaining 11.53% is irrigated by other source of irrigation. The gross irrigated area in 2022-23 was estimated at 122294 thousand hectares, which was 55.75% of the gross cropped area. Indian irrigation projects can be classified into three groups.

                                                                                  (i) Minor irrigation projects - Up to 2000 hectares of are irrigated under these projects. These include wells, tubewells, ponds, pumpsets, drip irrigation, sprinklers etc. Minor irrigation projects fulfill about 62% of the demand for irrigation in India.

                                                                                  (ii) Medium irrigation projects - More than 2000 to 10000 hectares of area are irrigated under these projects.

                                                                                  (iii) Major irrigation projects - More than 10,000 hectares of area are irrigated under these projects. 38% of the need for irrigation in the country is fulfilled by the major irrigation projects.

                                                                                  • Gang Canal is one of the world’s oldest and most developed canals. It was constructed in the year 1927 by Shri Ganga Singh, the then Maharaja of Bikaner. It arose from Hussaniwala, near the river Sutlej from Ferozepur.
                                                                                  • The Eastern Yamuna Canal originates from the left bank of Yamuna at Hathnikund Barrage. The length of the main canal is 197 kilometres. This canal system provides irrigation facility to Hindon, Yamuna Doab's, Saharanpur, Muzaffarnagar, Meerut and Ghaziabad. After its revival, the canal started functioning in 1830 A.D. At that time, the water discharged from this canal was about 800 cusecs. In the meantime, this was increased to about 4000 cusecs.
                                                                                  • The construction of Upper Ganga Canal was completed during the period of 1842 AD. Sir P.T. Cautley was the father of this project. The water was discharged for the first time on April 8, 1854, in this canal. It starts from a place called Bhimgoda in Haridwar on the right bank of the river Ganga. The length of the main canal is 298 km and the total length of this canal system is 6496 km. Irrigation facilities are being provided in Haridwar, Saharanpur, Muzaffarnagar, Meerut, Ghaziabad, Bulandshahr, Aligarh, Etah, Mathura, Firozabad, Mainpuri, and Agra districts by this canal system. Initially, this canal system was also used for waterways, in addition to irrigation. 200 cusecs of water from this canal system are provided to Delhi and about 100 cusecs water is given to Harduwaganj Thermal Power Plant.
                                                                                  • The sharda Major Canal has been constructed on the right bank of river Sarda near Banbasa in Champawat district in order to provide protective irrigation facilities to the districts of Pilibhit, Bareilly, Lakhimpur Kheri, Shahjahanpur, Hardoi, Unnao, Lucknow, Barabanki, Raebareli, Pratapgarh, Sultanpur, Jaunpur, Azamgarh, Ghazipur and Prayagraj. The length of the main canal is

                                                                                  44.3 km and the total length of the Sharda canal system is 9961.3 km.

                                                                                  • The lower Ganga canal starts from Narora (Bulandshahr). Its construction work was completed in 1878 A.D. The length of the main canal is 99.40 km. and the total length of the canal system is 8637.120 km.
                                                                                  • The foundation stone of the Indira Gandhi canal project was laid by the then Home Minister Govind Ballabh Pant in March, 1958. It originates from Harike Barrage situated at the confluence of the Sutlej and Beas rivers in Punjab. It is one of the world’s largest canal projects, with a total length of 649 km.
                                                                                  • The canal mainly irrigates Sri Ganganagar, Bikaner, Jodhpur and Jaisalmer districts of western Rajasthan.
                                                                                  • Under the Gandak project a 739 meter long barrage was built near the Triveni Ghat on Gandak River.
                                                                                  • The construction of Farakka Barrage was completed in the year 1975, with the aim of stopping the accumulation of silts in the Hooghly river. 40,000 cusecs of water from the Ganga river was diverted towards Hooghly river by a canal derived from the right bank of this barrage.
                                                                                  • Ten irrigation projects have been completed on the Bharatpujha river and its tributaries in the Palakkad district of Kerala. The Mangalam irrigation project is one of them.
                                                                                  • The Garland Canal system was proposed by Captain Dinshaw J. Dasthur, The whereas the idea of linking rivers was first proposed by irrigation engineer Vishweshwarya. Later, the name of K.L. Rao was added to it. The then Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee inaugurated the development plan “Hariyali”, related to water storage on January 27, 2003. Under this project, people are encouraged to conserve water in rural areas.
                                                                                  • On July 1, 2015, the Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sichayi Yojana (PMKSY) was approved to reduce the dependence of agriculture on monsoon and provide irrigation facilities to every farm. The Rural Development Ministry of the Government of India introduced three watershed development programmes untill April 1, 2008. These programmes are the Integrated Wastelands Development Programme, The Drought Prone Areas Programme and the Desert Development Programme. These programmes were brought under a comprehensive programme known as Integrated Watershed Management Programme.
                                                                                  • The main source of irrigation in Peninsular India is Pond. Since ancient times, ponds have been used for irrigation in these areas. The land of the Peninsular region is rocky; therefore, it is not possible to construct canals and wells easily. Besides, most of the rivers of Peninsular India are seasonal, which leads to a lack of water availability for canals. In this case, ponds serve as the main means of irrigation. According to data National Compilation on Dynamic Ground Water Resources of India, 2024. Uttar Pradesh (41.15 billion cubic m.), Punjab (26.24 billion cubic m.), Madhya Pradesh (17.90 billion cubic m.) and Maharashtra (15.07 billion cubic m.) are major states of India in terms of current annual groundwater extraction available for irrigation.
                                                                                  • According to the Statistical Diary Uttar Pradesh 2024 in the Uttar Pradesh (in 2022-23), in percentage of the net irrigated area by various means is Tubewell (74.1%), Canal (15.7%), Well (9.0%), Tanks, Pond and Lakes (0.6%) and by other means (0.6%).
                                                                                  • Tubewell is the most widespread means of irrigation in Uttar Pradesh.
                                                                                  Multi-Purpose River Valley Projects: key facts from the book

                                                                                  i- Narmada Valley Project:

                                                                                  • The Narmada is the fifth largest river in India. In 1946, a comprehensive program was drafted for irrigation, production of electricity and flood management in the Narmada Basin. In this project, 30 Major dams, 135 medium dams and 3000 minor dams on the Narmada and its tributaries were declared to be constructed.
                                                                                  • The Sardar Sarovar Project has been established on the Narmada river in Gujarat (163 Meters high near Navagam). It has an installed hydroelectric capacity of 1450 MW.
                                                                                  • There are two power houses for the Sardar Sarovar Project (SSP). (i) 1200 MW River Bed Power House and (ii) 250 MW Canal Head Power House. Power benefits are shared among Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Gujarat in the ratio of 57:27:16 respectively.
                                                                                  • The beneficiary states under the Narmada Water Disputes Tribunal (NWDT) water allocation for the Sardar Sarovar Project are madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Maharashtra and Rajasthan. Medha Patkar founded 'Narmada Dharanagrast' Samiti' in February 1986 with the objective of opposing this project. In 1989, several local organizations merged and named it the “Narmada Bachao Aandolan” (N.B.A.). The Narmada Sagar Project is also known as “Indira Sagar Project”. This dam is situated near Punasa in Khandwa district (M.P.) in Narmada town. The target of irrigation of 1.69 lakh Hectares annually and 1000 MW production of electricity has been set.
                                                                                  • There are several projects in the Narmada Valley, such as Tawa, Barna, Kolar, Sukta and Matiyari projects. The irrigation capacity of about 3,98,300 hectares of land has been attained through these projects.
                                                                                  • 13.50 MW of electricity is produced from the Tawa project.
                                                                                  • Various projects have been started at the tributaries of the river Narmada, such as the Man project at the Man river, Jobat (Shahid Chandra Shekhar Azad Sagar) project on Hathani river and Upper Veda project at the Veda river.
                                                                                  Multi-Purpose River Valley Projects · Bhakra Nangal Dam: key facts from the book
                                                                                  • Bhakra Nangal multi-purpose project is a joint venture for Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan.
                                                                                  • Under this, two dams have been constructed near Bhakra and Nangal on Satluj river. The construction of Bhakra Dam was completed in 1963.

                                                                                  Bhakra dam is located at a gorge near the upstream Bhakra Village in Bilaspur district of Himachal Pradesh, which is about 13 km upstream from Nangal Township. The canal command area of the Bhakra-Nangal extends into Punjab, haryana and Rajasthan; the Bhakra Dam itself is located in Himachal Pradesh. Water storage of this dam is done in Gobind Sagar Lake.

                                                                                  Multi-Purpose River Valley Projects · Dam at the River Cauvery: key facts from the book
                                                                                  • Development of Hydroelectricity started in last decade of the 19th century. In 1897, Hydropower plant was established in Sidrapong for electricity supply to Darjeeling. It is the oldest hydropower plant of India. The second oldest hydropower a plant was planted at Shivasamudram on Cauvery river in Karnataka in 1902. Shivsamudram is an ancient place. It is located in Cauvery Doab, near about 50 km northeast of Mysuru. Here, the water of Cauvery appears to be a great lake due to the morphology of the mountain.
                                                                                  • Krishna Sagar Dam is also situated at Cauvery river in Karnataka.
                                                                                  • The DPR or profile of this dam was prepared by M. Vishweshwaraiya.
                                                                                  • Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Kerala and Puducherry are parties in Cauvery dispute. According to decisions of Supreme Court (in 2018), of the total 740 (726+14) thousand million cubic feet of Cauvery water, 284.75 (270+14.75) TMC feet to have been allocated Karnataka, 30 thousand million cubic feet to Kerala, 404.25 (419-14.75) thousand million cubic feet to Tamil Nadu and 7 thousand million cubic feet to Puducherry.
                                                                                  Multi-Purpose River Valley Projects · Nagarjuna Sagar Dam: key facts from the book
                                                                                  • Nagarjuna Sagar multi-purpose project is established on the Krishna river. It was completed in 1967. It is located at the border of Telangana and Andhra Pradesh. The irrigation facility has been made available mainly to Nalgonda, Suryapet, Khammam (Telangana) and Guntur/Palnadu, Prakasam, Krishna, West Godavari etc. (Andhra Pradesh) through this project.
                                                                                  • The height of Nagarjuna Sagar dam is about 125 metre. Reservoir of Nagarjuna Sagar dam have the capacity of water storage 11550-11560 million cubic metres.
                                                                                  • As per the project, a about 1450 m long masonry dam has been constructed.
                                                                                  Multi-Purpose River Valley Projects · Hirakud Dam: key facts from the book

                                                                                  Hirakud Dam is a multipurpose project built on river Mahanadi in the Odisha State. This project was started in the year 1948 and Stage-I was completed in 1956. Hirakud Dam is situated 15 km North of Sambalpur district in Odisha, it is approx. 61m (200 ft) in height & 4801 m long. World longest earthen dam. The total length of Dam is 25.8 km.The project provides 155635 hectares of Kharif and 108385 hectares of Rabi irrigation.

                                                                                  Multi-Purpose River Valley Projects · Chambal Valley Project: key facts from the book
                                                                                  • Chambal river originates from Janapav hills near Mhow (Now- Dr. Ambedkar Nagar) in Madhya Pradesh. It meets the river Yamuna near Etawa. Chambal project is a joint venture of Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh. Under this project, three major dams have been constructed

                                                                                  1. Gandhi Sagar Dam (M.P.)

                                                                                  2. Rana Pratap Sagar Dam (Rajasthan)

                                                                                  3. Jawahar Sagar Dam (Rajasthan)

                                                                                  • Gandhi Sagar Dam project is the first among the four Chambal valley projects. This dam is established in Mandsaur district (M.P.). The height of this dam is 62.17 meter. The work was started in 1957 in the Power Station, while Power generation and its distribution commenced in November 1960.
                                                                                  • Rana Pratap Sagar Dam has been established in Rajasthan.
                                                                                  • Jawahar Sagar Dam was constructed 30 km far from Kota in Rajasthan.
                                                                                  Multi-Purpose River Valley Projects · Tehri Dam Project: key facts from the book
                                                                                  • The Tehri Dam project has been constructed on the Bhagirathi river in Tehri Garhwal district in Uttarakhand. The main objective of this project is storage of surplus monsoon water from the Bhilangana and Bhagirathi river for irrigation, flood control and electricity generation.
                                                                                  • It was approved in 1972 by the Planning commission but the work on it started in 1978. For this project THDC (Tehri Hydro Development Corporation Ltd.) was established.
                                                                                  • It is the highest dam of India (260.5 Meter). The main reason for the protest against the Tehri Dam project is its association to earthquake-prone area, damage of environment and displacement of local people.
                                                                                  Multi-Purpose River Valley Projects · Damodar Valley Project: key facts from the book
                                                                                  • Damodar river is the main tributary of Hugli. It is known as “Sorrow of Bengal” due to excessive pollution and frequent floods. Damodar Valley Corporation was established in 1948.
                                                                                  • The dam of Tilaiya, Belpahadi and Maithon has been constructed on Barakar River which is the tributary of Damodar River.
                                                                                  • Tilaiya dam is located in Koderma district. Construction of this dam was completed in 1953.
                                                                                  • Konar dam at Konar river in Hazaribag district is situated 24 km east from the confluence of Damodar. It was completed in the year 1955.
                                                                                  • Maithon dam is established at Barakar River. It was completed in 1957.
                                                                                  • Panchet hill dam is situated 20 km south of the Maithon Dam at Damodar River. It was completed in 1959.

                                                                                  Under this valley project (Damodar) two canals have been started from Durgapur Barrage. The lands of Howrah, Hugli and Vardhman (now Purba Bardhaman & Paschim Bardhaman) are irrigated by these canals.

                                                                                        Multi-Purpose River Valley Projects · Miscellaneous Projects: key facts from the book
                                                                                        • In India, multi-purpose river valley projects, besides irrigation, also facilitates flood control, water supply, hydroelectric generation, tourism, canals etc. The first hydropower plant was established in 1897 in Darjeeling (W. Bengal) near Sidrapong.
                                                                                        • Chukha Hydroelectric project was constructed with the help of India in Bhutan. Chukha dam is established at the upper part of Raidak river or Wang Chu river in Bhutan. The height of this dam is 40 meters. In 1974, construction work of this dam by the Indian government was started as a fully funded unit in which 60% is in the form of grant and 40% in the form of a loan. The loan has to be paid at the annual rate of 5% in 15 years. This project was handed over to Bhutan in 1991.It has a capacity of 336 Megawatt.
                                                                                        • Bhakra Nangal Dam project is established at Satluj River. This is a combined project of Punjab, Haryana, and Rajasthan.
                                                                                        • Hirakud dam project is established at Mahanadi river in Odisha. Three dams (Hirakud, Tikar Pada and Naraj) have been constructed on the lines of this project.
                                                                                        • Idukki dam project has been set up at Periyar River in Kerala. Nagarjuna Sagar dam project has been established at Krishna river.
                                                                                        • Telugu-Ganga Project is a joint venture of Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka. This project provides water supply from the Krishna river to the city of Chennai (Tamil Nadu).
                                                                                        • Mettur Project has been established at Cauvery river in Tamil Nadu.
                                                                                        • West Bengal and Jharkhand both are benefitted from Mayurakshi Project.
                                                                                        • Canada Dam (Massanjore dam) has been constructed at Mayurakshi river in Jharkhand under this project.
                                                                                        • Baglihar Hydroelectric Power Project is established at Chenab river in Ramban district in Jammu and Kashmir.
                                                                                        • Daman Ganga Irrigation Project is established at Daman Ganga River Valsad district 30 km far from Vapi in the Southern Gujarat. Girna Irrigation Project is constructed at Girna River in Nashik district in Maharashtra.
                                                                                        • Pamba Irrigation Project is establishes at Pamba river in Pathanamthitta district of Kerala. Baira Siul Hydropower electric project has been established at siul river in Chamba district, of Himachal Pradesh. Suil is tributary of Ravi river.
                                                                                        • Dulhasti Hydro-power Station is situated at Chenab river in Kishtwar district of Jammu and Kashmir.
                                                                                        • Rajghat dam project at Betwa river in Lalitpur is known as Rani Laxmibai Sagar. Tilaiya Dam is situated at Bara kar river in Koderma district of Jharkhand.
                                                                                        • Kishau Dam is being built at the Tons river (a tributary Yamuna). Tons river flows through the border of Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand. Main beneficiary states from this project are Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh and Union Territory of Delhi.
                                                                                        • Babli Project is a highly disputed project between Maharashtra and Telangana at Godavari River.
                                                                                        • Tapovan Vishnugad Hydroelectric Project is under construction at Dhauliganga river in Chamoli district of Uttarakhand.
                                                                                        • Mahakali Treaty between India and Nepal was held in February 1996. The treaty determined the limit of use of water from Mahakali or Sharda river. Sharda Barrage, Tanakpur Barrage and proposed Pancheswar Project are within the periphery of this treaty.

                                                                                        In 1959, there was a treaty between India and Nepal on construction of Gandak Barrage. The objective of this barrage is to provide irrigation and Power development facility in Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Nepal.

                                                                                        • Kalpong hydro electric power project is the first hydro electric hydroelectric power project of Andaman and Nicobar Island. It is situated at Kalpong river.
                                                                                        • Rihand dam project is also known as Govind Ballav Pant Sagar Project. It was built at Rihand river at Pipri in Sonbhadra (U.P.). The length of this dam is 934.45 meter and its height is about 91.46 meters. A hydroelectric station of300 Megawatt capacity has been built below the dam in Obra. An artificial lake named Govind Ballav Pant Sagar has also been constructed under this project. It is the largest project of Uttar Pradesh.
                                                                                        • Ukai dam is multi-purpose project of Gujarat 94 km far from Surat. It has been built at Tapti River in Ukai.
                                                                                        • Kalagarh dam is built at Ramganga River. Its length is 715 meter and height is 128 meter. Koyna dam is built at Koyna river which is located in Maharashtra.
                                                                                        • Tawa project is located at Narmada Puram district of Madhya Pradesh on Tawa river. Tawa reservoir is nestled between the western boundary of Satpura National Park and Bori Wildlife Sanctuary.
                                                                                        • The Pong dam has been constructed on the Beas river Himachal Pradesh. It is also known as Beas dam. Maharana Pratap Sagar lake created by this dam was later declared a bird sanctuary.
                                                                                        • Meja dam has been constructed on the Kothari river near Meja village in Bhilwara district of Rajasthan.
                                                                                        • Kothari is a tributary of river Banas. This dam is mainly used for irrigation. Tulbul navigable project has been built at Jhelum river in Jammu & Kashmir.
