                                                                                                                                                                                              The Universe · The Solar System: key facts from the book
                                                                                                                                                                                              • The family of the ‘Sun’ is known as the solar system. Eight major planets, dwarf planets, satellites and countless minor bodies (asteroids, meteors, and comets) orbit the Sun to form the solar system. The solar system dates back to about 4.6 billion years.
                                                                                                                                                                                              • Originally there were 9 planets in the solar system. Their average distance in ascending order from the Sun is as follows –

                                                                                                                                                                                              1. Mercury (57.9 million km)

                                                                                                                                                                                              2. Venus (108.2 million km)

                                                                                                                                                                                              3. Earth (149.6 million km)

                                                                                                                                                                                              4. Mars (228 million km)

                                                                                                                                                                                              5. Jupiter (778.5 million km)

                                                                                                                                                                                              6. Saturn (1432 million km)

                                                                                                                                                                                              7. Uranus (2867 million km)

                                                                                                                                                                                              8. Neptune (4515 million km)

                                                                                                                                                                                              9. Pluto (5906.4 million km)

                                                                                                                                                                                              Note- Between 14-25 August, 2006 the 26th General Assembly of the International Astronomical Union was held in Prague (Czech Republic). The assembly excluded Pluto from the list of planets and reclassified it as a dwarf planet.

                                                                                                                                                                                              • Planets differ from each other depending on their size, composition, temperature and time taken for a revolution. The main reason for this difference is their distance from the sun.
                                                                                                                                                                                              • Some planets like Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are solid; these planets are called terrestrial planets whereas some planets have a gaseous composition like Jupiter and Saturn. Due to their large size these planets are also known as Jovian Planets (Jovian means like Jupiter).
                                                                                                                                                                                              • Out of all the 8 planets, Earth has the maximum mean density i.e. 5.5 g/cm³. The mean density of other planets is as follows –

                                                                                                                                                                                              Mercury (5.4 g/cm³), Venus (5.2 g/cm³), Mars (3.9 g/cm³), Jupiter (1.3 g/cm³), Saturn (0.7 g/cm³), Uranus (1.3 g/cm³), Neptune (1.6 g/cm³).

                                                                                                                                                                                              • The Sun alone carries 99.8% of the total mass of the solar system.
                                                                                                                                                                                              • Sun’s mass is 1.989 × 10³⁰ kilograms which is 3,33000 times that of the planet Earth.
                                                                                                                                                                                              • Mercury is the smallest planet of the solar system whereas Jupiter is the largest.
                                                                                                                                                                                              • Venus is the brightest planet whereas Neptune is the farthest. Neptune takes the maximum time in to complete one revolution around the Sun (165 yrs).
                                                                                                                                                                                              • The descending order of planets according to their size is as follows - Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, Earth, Venus, Mars, Mercury.
                                                                                                                                                                                              • The descending order of the planets according to their mass is as follows – Jupiter, Saturn, Neptune, Uranus, Earth, Venus, Mars & Mercury.
                                                                                                                                                                                              • The ascending order of planets according to their distance from the Sun is as follows
                                                                                                                                                                                              • – Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.
                                                                                                                                                                                              • Among all the planets, Jupiter has the maximum gravitational acceleration (23.1 m/s²).
                                                                                                                                                                                              • Gases like hydrogen and helium are found in abundance on planets like Jupiter and Saturn. The Goldilocks zone is also called the habitable zone. In astronomy, the Goldilocks zone is the range of the orbits around a star within which a planetary surface can support liquid water given sufficient atmospheric pressure. Liquid water is one of the most important elements in finding life on other planets. Earth is the only known life-supporting planet in the solar system, and it lies in the Sun's Goldilocks zone. This zone is neither too hot nor too cold.
                                                                                                                                                                                              • By 1514, Polish astronomer and mathematician Ncolaus Copernicus had written the handwritten essay 'Commentariolus' (Little Commentary). In this essay, he gave information regarding the principle of revolution. According to this essay, the Sun is at the center of the universe and earth revolves around it. Later in 1543 AD, it was been published by the name 'De revolutionibus orbium coelestium (On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres).
                                                                                                                                                                                              • It is noteworthy to mention that in 6th century A.D. i.e. 1000 years before Nicolaus Copernicus. The famous Indian astronomer Varamihira had already proposed the theory that, the Moon revolves around the Earth and Earth revolves around the Sun.
                                                                                                                                                                                              • Johannes Kepler was a German astronomer, mathematician and astrologer. He is best known for propounding the ‘three laws of planetary motion’.
                                                                                                                                                                                              • Galileo Galilei, the famous scientist of Italy gave us the fundamental principles of falling bodies.
                                                                                                                                                                                              • English scientist Isaac Newton gave us the fundamental principles of velocity and also discovered the laws of gravity.
                                                                                                                                                                                              The Universe · The Sun: key facts from the book
                                                                                                                                                                                              • The sun is the centre of our solar system. The bright outer layer that emits most of the radiation, particularly the visible light is known as the Photosphere.
                                                                                                                                                                                              • According to NASA the diameter of the sun is 109.2 times bigger than our planet earth. The mean radius of the sun is 695700 km. Due to the very high temperature in the sun’s core (appx. 15,000,000 oC) every matter present in it is either in a gaseous state or in the plasma state.
                                                                                                                                                                                              • Plasma is the 4th state of matter after solid, liquid and gas. As per NASA, the surface temperature of the sun is 5500°C. The entire source of the Sun’s energy is a result of nuclear fusion- the fusing of hydrogen into helium, creating energy.
                                                                                                                                                                                              • Nuclear reactions are of two types- nuclear fusion and nuclear fission.
                                                                                                                                                                                              • In nuclear fusion, two or more atomic nuclei are combined to form one or more different atomic nuclei and subatomic particles (neutrons or protons).
                                                                                                                                                                                              • Nuclear fission is a reaction in which a heavy nucleus splits spontaneously or on impact with another particle, with the release of energy. The release of energy from the stars is due to nuclear fusion. In stars when the temperature reaches between 1 to 1.5 crore Celsius. The atoms of hydrogen fuse together to form helium.

                                                                                                                                                                                              H2 + H2 He4 + Energy

                                                                                                                                                                                              Deuterium Helium

                                                                                                                                                                                              • Solar eclipse is a situation when the complete or partial hiding of the sun is caused by the moon’s passing between the sun and the earth. A solar eclipse occurs only on a new moon day. The outer layer of the sun which is visible during a solar eclipse is known as the corona. In any circumstances, the maximum duration of a total solar eclipse cannot exceed
                                                                                                                                                                                              • 7.5 minutes.
                                                                                                                                                                                              • When a solar flare enters the atmosphere of our planet, they collide with the air particles and produces a beautiful display of a light show especially in the regions of upper latitude. This display is known as Aurora lights. At North Pole it is called Aurora Borealis and at the South Pole, it is called Aurora Australis.
                                                                                                                                                                                              • A dark patch on the surface of the sun is known as a sunspot. Sunspots appear as regions with temperature about 1500K cooler than the surrounding photospheres.
                                                                                                                                                                                              • We can often witness a white color ring around the sun and the moon, it is known as a halo. It is caused when the light gets refracted or reflected due to the presence of cirrus and cirrostratus clouds in the upper layers of the atmosphere. The distance between the sun and the earth is minimum in the first week of January, this situation or position is called 'Perihelion'. Generally Perihelion occurs on 4th January. While opposite to it is on 4th July, the sun stands farthest from the earth and this position or situation is known as 'Aphelion'.
                                                                                                                                                                                              • Astronomical unit is used for measuring distance or length. For general reference, we can say that one Astronomical unit represents the mean distance between the earth and the sun (149.598 ×10⁶ km or 149.6×10⁶ km). In meters it is 149.59 × 10⁹; In millimetres it is 149.59 × 10¹².
                                                                                                                                                                                              The Universe · The Mercury: key facts from the book
                                                                                                                                                                                              • It is the smallest planet of the solar system and is nearest to the sun. It completes its one revolution in around 88 days.
                                                                                                                                                                                              • Mercury and Venus are the planets having no satellites.
                                                                                                                                                                                              • The absence of atmosphere makes it impossible for the sustenance of any life on Mercury.
                                                                                                                                                                                              • The average range of temperature on Mercury is around 167°C.
                                                                                                                                                                                              • Mariner 10 was a satellite launched by NASA that traveled very close to Mercury and took photos of the planet. From the pictures, it was found that the surface of the planet Mercury has a number of mountains and plains. The distance between the Sun and Mercury is approx. 57.9 million km or 0.39 AU.
                                                                                                                                                                                              • All the 8 planets of the solar system revolve around the sun. The time taken for one revolution around the sun, by every planet is as follows – Mercury (88 days), Venus (224.7 days), Earth (365.2 days), Mars (687 days), Jupiter (11.86 years), Saturn (29.4 yrs), Uranus (84.07 yrs), Neptune (164.9 yrs).
                                                                                                                                                                                              • Albedo is an expression of the ability of surfaces to reflect sunlight (heat from the Sun).
                                                                                                                                                                                              • Light coloured surfaces return a large part of the sun’s rays back to space (high albedo). Dark surfaces absorb the rays from the sun (low albedo). Hence, Albedo determines the brightness of a body.
                                                                                                                                                                                              • Mercury receives a very high amount of sunlight but its albedo is low as compared to earth hence the planet Mercury is not that bright in nature.
                                                                                                                                                                                              • The albedo of Earth is 0.3 whereas the albedo of Mercury is mere 0.1. The diameter of planet Mercury is appx. 4879 km.
                                                                                                                                                                                              The Universe · The Venus: key facts from the book
                                                                                                                                                                                              • Venus is also known as the twin sister of planet Earth. Venus is the brightest planet as seen from Earth, in night sky. It is also known as the Morning Star and Evening Star. The average distance from the Sun is appx 108.2 million km. It is the second closest planet to our sun. It takes Venus appx. 225 (224.7) days to complete its one revolution. It is the hottest planet in the solar system with an average temperature of 464°C (737K).
                                                                                                                                                                                              • The temperature of the planets in the solar system is as follows –
                                                                                                                                                                                              Mercury=167 °C,
                                                                                                                                                                                              Venus=464 °C
                                                                                                                                                                                              Earth=15 °C,
                                                                                                                                                                                              Mars=–65 °C,
                                                                                                                                                                                              Jupiter=–110 °C,
                                                                                                                                                                                              Saturn=–140 °C,
                                                                                                                                                                                              Uranus=–195 °C,
                                                                                                                                                                                              Neptune=–200 °C.
                                                                                                                                                                                              • Every planet in our solar system except for Venus and Uranus rotates clockwise i.e., from east to west.
                                                                                                                                                                                              • Venus has a thick atmosphere. The atmosphere of Venus mainly comprises of carbon-dioxide (about 96.5%), with average temperatures increasing above 400°C. That is why the planet experiences a pressure cooker like condition. Hence because of the above conditions sustenance of any life form becomes next to impossible on this planet.
                                                                                                                                                                                              • Just like Mercury & Venus too has no natural satellite of its own.
                                                                                                                                                                                              • In the year 1989 Magellan spacecraft was sent to Venus on a deep space mission for the next 4 years i.e., from 1990-1994. It observed the planet Venus and its features. The satellite was named after Ferdinand Magellan, a famous Portuguese explorer of the 16th century.

                                                                                                                                                                                              Nebula → not part of the solar system; solar system (formed about 4.6 billion years ago) has the Sun, planets, dwarf planets, asteroids, comets, meteoroids.

                                                                                                                                                                                                    The Universe · The Earth: key facts from the book
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • The Earth is the third planet from the sun behind Mercury and Venus respectively. It is located between Venus and Mars. Survival of life is possible on our planet because of its ecology. Hence Earth has been given the name Green Planet.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • Greek Philosopher Aristotle (384-322 B.C.) has clearly mentioned in second volume of the 14th chapter of his book "On The Heavens". But now it is universally accepted that the shape of our planet is much closer to being an oblate spheroid. Hence, the shape of our planet is called Geoid (Geoid meaning earth like).
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • Our planet Earth is tilted on its axis at an angle of 23⁰30'.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • The Earth takes 24 hours to rotate once on its axis. This leads to the phenomena of Day and Night.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • Basically that part of the planet which is facing the sun experiences day and the opposite side experiences night.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • The axial tilt of 23⁰30' (now 23⁰44') as it moves around the Sun causes seasonal changes.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • The moon is an astronomical body that orbits planet Earth and is Earth’s only permanent natural satellite.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • On 21st March and 23rd September the Sun shines directly above the equator twice. From 21st March to 23rd September (6 months) the Sun shines between the equator and tropic of cancer. Thus, the Northern Hemisphere experiences summers and the Southern Hemisphere experiences winters.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • On the other hand, the next 6 months i.e. from 23rd September to 21st of March the sun shines between the equator and the tropic of Capricorn. Hence, the southern hemisphere experiences summers and the northern hemisphere experiences winters.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • Because of the slanted rays falling on the hemisphere, opposite to the one receiving direct sunlight, at any point north of the Arctic Circle or south of the Antarctic Circle there will be one period in the summer when the sun does not set, and one period in winter when the sun does not rise. For example in Northern Hemisphere the sun does not set at the North Pole and vice-versa.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • On June 21st, the sun is directly overhead the Tropic of Cancer. This phenomenon is known as the Summer Solstice. On 22nd December, the sun is directly overhead the Tropic of Capricorn. This phenomenon is called the Winter Solstice.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • The 45-degree latitude is often called the halfway point between the equator and the North Pole. The cosine 45 latitude equals to 0.707, hence the length of this latitude is
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • 0.707 × 40090.2857 = 28343.832 km. Therefore, the length of the 45° latitude is more than half of the length of the equator. The length of 60-degree latitude is half the length of the equator (cosine 60° = 0.5). The circumference of the equator is appx. 40090 km. Whereas the equatorial diameter of the Earth is appx. 12800 (12756 km).
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • The rotation of the Earth creates a centrifugal force which is maximum at the equator. As a result of this force, the weight of any object is minimum at the equator and increases with an increase in latitudes and is maximum at the poles.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • The movement of the Earth in its orbit around the sun is called a revolution. It takes Earth 365.25 Days or 365 Days, 6 hours 9 minutes and
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • 9.51 seconds to complete one revolution.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • A tropical year (also known as a solar year) is the time that the Sun takes to return to the same position in the cycles of the seasons, as seen from Earth; for example, the time from the Vernal equinox to Vernal equinox or from summer solstice to summer solstice.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • The one tropical year is approx. 365.24 days. Normally a calendar is based on a tropical year, which is 365 days, 5 hours, 48 min. and 45.2 seconds long.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • The year 2000 AD witnessed an increase of 5 minutes in the length of the year. The length of the year was 365 days, 6 hours, 13 min. and 53.26 seconds. These types of years are called Anomalistic years.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • The Earth revolves around the Sun at an average speed of 29.78 km/sec (appx. 30km/sec). The revolution speed of the other planets in the solar system is as follows – (1) Mercury 47.4 km/s, (2) Venus – 35 km/s, (3) Earth – 29.78 km/s (4) Mars – 24.1 km/s

                                                                                                                                                                                                    (5) Jupiter – 13.1 km/s, (6) Saturn – 9.7 km/s (7) Uranus – 6.8 km/s (8) Neptune – 5.4 km/s.

                                                                                                                                                                                                    • The average distance between the sun and the Earth is 149597870.7 km. It takes appx. 8 min. and 19 seconds for the Sun’s rays to reach our planet. These electromagnetic energy waves travel at a speed of186282 miles/sec. The closest star to Earth is the Sun. The distance of other stars from our planet Earth is as follows– (1) Alpha Centauri - 4.35 light years, (2) Sun – 149.6 × 10⁶ km, (3) Sirius A (Dog Star) – 8.6 light years.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • The Earth’s magnetic field varies from place to place. Thumba is an ideal location for satellites as a result, The Thumba Equatorial Rocket Launching Station was established here.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • Thumba is located in Thiruvananthapuram, the district of Kerala.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • The projection of maximum artificial satellites is towards the east of the planet Earth. This is because a satellite launched towards the east direction will get an initial boost equal to the velocity of the earth surface. Thus, the initial boost helps in cutting down the cost of rockets used to launch the satellite. However, a satellite is not always projected towards the east. Such satellites that are to be placed in polar orbits are launched in the south or north directions.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • The inner core of our planet is solid. The outer core is in liquid form. The core has a depth of 2900 km.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • The crust is composed of different elements in varied proportions. They are as follows (according to percentage by weight) - Oxygen (O) – 46.60%, Silicon (Si) – 27.72%, Aluminium (Al) – 8.13%, Iron (Fe) – 5.00%, Calcium (Ca) – 3.63%, Sodium (Na)- 2.83 %, Potassium (K) – 2.59%, Magnesium (Mg) – 2.09%.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • Earth Day is an annual event celebrated on April 22 worldwide. It was first observed in the year 1970.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    The Universe · The Mars: key facts from the book
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • Mars is the fourth planet from the sun third being Earth.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • The axial tilt of Mars is 25°12' relative to its orbital plane.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • Mars average distance from the Sun is roughly 227943824 km (228 million km) and its orbital period is 687.0 Earth days. The diameter of Mars is 6792 km and it takes 24.7 hours to complete one rotation.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • The atmospheric composition of Mars is CO₂- 95.1%, N₂-2.59%, Argon - 1.94%, Oxygen -
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • 0.16% and traces of water.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO), took pictures of Mars with the help of its hi tech cameras. After studying the pictures, scientists were able to claim the presence of liquid water on Mars.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • The MRO contains a host of scientific instruments such as imaging spectrometers that helped in finding the hydrated minerals of the planet. The average temperature of Mars, it is – 65°C (208 K).
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • Mars and Earth are very different planets when it comes to temperature, size and atmosphere, but original processes on the two Planets are surprisingly similar.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • Mars is often referred to as the Red planet because the reddish iron oxide prevalent on its surface gives it a reddish appearance.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • Mars has two relatively small natural moons, Phobos and Deimos.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • The Olympus Mons (formerly Nix Olympica) mountain (volcano) of Mars is approx. three times the size of our Mount Everest.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • The Phoenix Mars Lander was a space exploration mission of NASA on Mars under the Scout program. It was launched on August 4th, 2007 and landed on Mars on May 25th, 2008. The mission was declared concluded on November 2, 2008. Phoenix was the first lander that gave valuable inputs regarding the presence of ice on the planet.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • The Curiosity Rover was launched by NASA to explore the possibility of life, determine the role of water, and study the climate and geology of Mars. The Mars Orbiter Mission (MOM) or Mangalyaan is India’s first Mars exploration mission. It was launched on 5th November 2013 by the Indian Space Research Organization (ISRO). It was launched with the help of the PSLV- C25 rocket. It was inserted into Mars’s orbit on 24 September 2014. Now, with the success of the MoM mission India has become a member of the elite Mars club (United States of America, Russia, European Union).
                                                                                                                                                                                                    The Universe · The Jupiter: key facts from the book
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun and the largest in the solar system. Its diameter is 142984 km. The average density of Jupiter is 1326 kg/m³.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • The descending order of planets in the solar system as per their diameter is as follows
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • – Jupiter (142984 km), Saturn (120536 km),, Uranus (51118 km), Neptune (49528 km), Earth (12756km), Venus (12104 km), Mars (6792 km), Mercury (4879 km).
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • It takes Jupiter

                                                                                                                                                                                                    11.86 years to complete one revolution around the sun.

                                                                                                                                                                                                    • As of 27 January 2026, 97 satellites of Jupiter have been discovered. Among these, the 4 largest satellites of Jupiter are Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto. These four are also known as Galilean Moons. They were first seen by Galileo Galilei in January 1610 and recognized by him as satellites of Jupiter.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • Ganymede is the largest and most massive moon of Jupiter and in the solar system. Jupiter is also known as miniature solar system. Voyager-1 spacecraft was sent to explore the Jovian system in 1977. It explored Europa (one of the four Galilean moons). It provided detailed images of Europa’s icy surface. Hence causing many scientists to speculate about the possibility of a liquid ocean similar to those found on Earth. These liquid oceans possibly have a depth of appx. 60-150 km.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • If it is proven then Europa will be the only place in the solar system apart from our planet Earth where water is present in that quantity.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • Jupiter’s ring was first discovered by the Voyager 1 spacecraft in 1979. These rings are also known as Jovian Rings. These rings are mostly made of silicate and dust particles. It is because of the transparency that these rings are difficult to spot however their existence cannot be questioned. Jupiter is primarily composed of hydrogen and helium. Some traces of methane, ammonia hydrogen deuteride, ethanel etc. is are also found. Jupiter is the fastest spinning planet in the solar system.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    The Universe · The Saturn: key facts from the book
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • Saturn is the sixth planet from the sun and the second largest in the solar system. It has 274 natural satellites.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • Titan is its largest satellite, having a diameter of 5150 km.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • Rhea is the second largest natural satellite of Saturn having a diameter of 1528 km.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • Other natural satellites of Saturn include Dione, Tethys, Mimas, Enceladus, Lapetus, Helene, Atlas, etc. It takes Saturn about 29.4 years to finish one revolution around the sun.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • Saturn is also known as ‘Globe of Gases’ and ‘Galaxy Like Planet’.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • Saturn is probably best known for the system of planetary rings that make it visually unique. Planetary rings A,B,D and E of the planet Saturn are visible from Earth.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • The most prominent and most famous planetary rings in the solar system are those around Saturn, but the other three giant planets Jupiter, Uranus, and Neptune also have a ring system.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • Saturn appears to the naked eye in the night sky as a bright, yellowish point of light. The duration of a day on Saturn is 10 hours 34 minutes and the planet's axial tilt is 26°70'. The average surface temperature of Saturn is –140°C.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • The atmosphere of Saturn contains, hydrogen and helium. Trace amounts of methane, hydrogen Deuteride, ethane etc. Ammonia has also been detected in saturns atmosphere.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • The magnetic field of saturn's is 578 times as powerful that of our planet Earth. The Phoebe satellite of Saturn orbits Saturn opposite to Saturn’s rotation.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • The Cassini probe was sent on 15th October, 1997 to orbit the planet Saturn.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    The Universe · The Uranus, Neptune and Pluto: key facts from the book
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • Uranus is the 7th planet from the Sun and the third largest planet in the solar system. Uranus was discovered by Sir William Herschel on 13th March 1781. The axial tilt or equatorial inclination of Uranus is 97.77°. Like Venus, Uranus rotates east to west. Uranus takes about 17 hours and 14 minutes to rotate on its axis, and about 84 Earth years to complete an orbit of the Sun (a Uranian year).
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • On Uranus, the Sun rises in the west and sets in the east.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • The composition of Uranus atmosphere is different from its bulk, consisting mainly of molecular hydrogen, helium, methane and ammonia etc..
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • Due to its distance from the Sun, Uranus is an ice giant and appears to be blue-green in colour due to presence of methane in its atmosphere. Uranus has 29 (as of March, 2025) moons. Just like Saturn, Uranus also has planetary rings.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • Neptune was discovered by German astronomer Johann Gottfried Galle on the night of 23-24 September 1846. One day on Neptune takes about 16 hours and 6 minutes (the time it takes for Neptune to rotate), and Neptune makes a complete orbit around the sun in about 164.9 years. Neptune’s axis of rotation is tilted at 28.3° with respect to the plane of its orbit around the sun.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • Neptune is the coldest planet in the solar system with an average temperature of-200°C. Neptune does not have a solid surface. Its atmosphere is mostly made up of hydrogen, helium and methane.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • Neptune has 16 known natural satellites among these Triton and Nereid are the prominent one.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • In 2006 when Pluto was excluded from the category of planets, Neptune became the farthest planet in the solar system.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • Pluto was discovered by Clyde Tombaugh in 1930. It was considered to be the smallest and the 9th planet of the solar system.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • Between 14 to 25 August 2006, the 26th General Assembly of the International Astronomical Union was held in Prague (Czech Republic). The assembly excluded Pluto from the list of planets and reclassified it as a dwarf planet. This was because the orbit of Pluto was overlapping with that of Neptune.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • Pluto has five known natural satellites. The closest to Pluto is Charon, followed by Styx, Nix, Kerberos and Hydra. Charon is the largest natural 'satellite' of Pluto. Pluto takes about 247.9 years to complete one revolution around the sun.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    The Universe · The Moon: key facts from the book
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • The moon is an astronomical body that orbits planet Earth and is Earth’s only permanent natural satellite. The diameter of the Moon is 3,475 km.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • The minimum and maximum distance between the Earth and Moon is 363300 km and 405500 km respectively.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • The Moon makes a complete orbit around Earth once every 27 days, 7 hours and 43 minutes. It is the same time that is taken by the Moon to complete its one rotation. The moon is tilted on its axis, due to which its appearance (size) changes with its distance from the Earth. Because of this effect, about 59% of the Moon’s surface can actually be seen from Earth.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • Sound requires a medium to travel. Since there is no atmosphere on the Moon, When two astronomers talk to each other it is not audible.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • Solar eclipses occur at the new moon, when the moon comes in between the sun and the earth. In contrast, lunar eclipses occur at full moon, when the earth is in between the sun and the moon. The type and duration of a lunar eclipse depend upon the orbital tilt and alignment of the moon.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • When the moon is closest to Earth (363300 km), then this condition is called perigee. It is during this time that high tides occur, because the gravitational pull of the moon is at its maximum. When the moon is at its farthest distance from the earth, the condition is called apogee. This is the time when low tides occur because the gravitational pull of the Moon is minimum.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • The low tides are 20% smaller than the high tides.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • A lunar perigee occurred on December 22nd, 1999 due to which the moon appeared to be the brightest. Again on November 14th, 2016 a full perigee occurred due to which the moon for the first time in over 60 years appeared to be the largest and the brightest. In common language, this phenomenon is known as supermoon. A supermoon occurs when the full moon coincides with the moon's orbit being closest (perigee) to Earth.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • During a supermoon, the moon appears roughly 14%, larger in diameter and 30% brighter.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • During a total lunar eclipse, earth completely blocks direct sunlight from reaching the moon. The only light reflected from the lunar surface has been refracted by Earth’s Atmosphere. Due to the reddish colour, a totally eclipsed moon is sometimes called a blood moon.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • A Blue Moon is an additional full moon that appears in a subdivision of a year-either as the third or fourth full moon in a season or a second full moon in a month of the common calendar. One lunar month is around 29.5 days long. Ifwe multiply 29.5 days by 12 months we get 354 days, which means there could be 12 full moons in a year. Since 11 days are still left in a year, approximately every 2.7154 years the condition for a Blue moon (one extra full moon) comes into existence. In every 2.7154 years there would be a month that has two full moons, however the difference between these two full moons will always be 29.5 days. Traditionally the second full moon of the month is called a Blue Moon.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • Accordingly in the year 2009 there were two full moons in December, one on 2nd December and one on 31st December. The one that occurred on 31st December was called a Blue Moon.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • According to the new definition of the Almanac the Blue Moon phenomenon is the occurrence of one extra full moon in an astronomical season. There are four astronomical seasons in a year- starting from 21st March to 23rd September (the Equinoxes) and the other two starting from 21st June to 22nd December (summer and winter solstice respectively). Hence the astronomical seasons are like this –

                                                                                                                                                                                                    1st Astronomical season (21st March to 20th June)

                                                                                                                                                                                                    2nd Astronomical season (21st June to 22nd September) 3rd Astronomical season (23rd September to 21st December) 4th Astronomical season (22nd December to 20th March) Every season is divided into 3 months. Hence every season will normally have 3 full moons, however in every 2.7154 years, one of the above 4 seasons will have 4 full moons instead of3. The astronomical season that has the 4th full moon will be known as the season with the Blue Moon. It is to be noted however that the 3rd full moon will be considered as the Blue moon and not the 4th one. It is because only then will the names of the other full moons, such as the moon before the solstice and the Moon after the solstice, fall at the proper times relative to the solstices and equinoxes. Hence, according to the above definition, the year 2010 witnessed 4 full moons the astronomical season starting from 23rd September to 22nd December. 25th September, 24th October, 21st November and 20th December witnessed full moons. The full moon of21st November 2010 was referred to as a Blue Moon.

                                                                                                                                                                                                    • The weight of any body on a planet or satellite depends upon the mass of the body and the gravitational acceleration of the planet. (Weight = mass × gravitational acceleration). The gravitational acceleration on the moon is 1/6th of that of planet Earth. Hence, any body or object taken to the moon has its weight reduced to 1/6th of its weight on planet Earth. The area of the large black patch as seen from the Earth is called Lunar Mare or Sea of Tranquility. It was the landing site for the first crewed landing on the Moon on July 20, 1969. Astronauts Neil Armstrong and Edwin Buzz Aldrin Junior made a smooth touchdown in the Apollo 11 Lunar Module named Eagle. The third astronaut on this mission was Michael Collins, however, he did not step on the Moon.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • The Apollo 11 returned to Earth and splashed down in the Pacific Ocean on July 24, 1969. The mission brought back substances from the surface of the Moon which weighed around 47 pounds. It was used for research purposes.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • Chandrayaan-1 was India’s first lunar probe. It was launched by the Indian Space Research Organisation on 22 October, 2008 and operated until August 2009. India launched the space craft using a PSLV-XL rocket (PSLV-C11). The vehicle was inserted into lunar orbit on 8 November 2008.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) set up a Indian Deep Space Network (IDSN) centre in Byalalu (Bengaluru) to track Chandrayaan-1.
                                                                                                                                                                                                    • Chandrayaan-2 is India’s second lunar exploration mission after Chandrayaan-1 developed by the Indian Space Research Organisation, the mission was launched to the Moon by a Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle Mk III - M1 (GSLV-MkIII-M1) on July 22, 2019. Chandrayaan-3 mission took off on July 14, 2023 from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Andhra Pradesh. On August 5, 2023 the mission entered lunar orbit. On August 17, the lander module separated from the propulsion module. The first and second deboosting occurred on August 18 and 20 respectively. OnAugust 23, 2023 the lander landed on the south pole of the Moon. India's third lunar mission, Chandrayaan - 3 made history in August, 2023 by successfully achieving a soft landing on the south pole of the Moon.

                                                                                                                                                                                                    With this, India became the first nation to land on the Moon's south pole and the fourth (after Russia, U.S.A. and China) to land successfully on Earth's only natural satellite.

                                                                                                                                                                                                    Aristotle (384-322 BC) → first to describe Earth as spherical, in 'On the Heavens'; Ptolemy, Strabo and Copernicus came later.
