                                                                                                                                                                                                                The Earth · Origin of the Earth: key facts from the book
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Earth is one of the planets in the solar system. Its origin is not different from that of the other planets. Different scholars have propounded different theories regarding the subject.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • One of the earliest works on the subject was presented by Immanuel Kant. He propounded the theory of nebulous material.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • In 1755 A.D. Immanuel Kant presented the Gaseous hypothesis. Later in 1796 A.D., Laplace presented his research on the topic which came to be known as Nebular Hypothesis. In 1905 A.D. Chamberlin and Moulton proposed the Chamberlin-Moulton planetesimal hypothesis to describe the formation of the solar system. The theory was based on the idea that a star passed close enough to the sun early in its life to cause tidal bulges to form on its surface, causing the material to be ejected repeatedly from the sun. Due to the gravitational effects of the passing star, materials would cool and condense into numerous small bodies, which they called planets.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • In 1919 the famous British scientist James Jeans propounded the Tidal Hypothesis and another scientist Sir Harold Jeffreys made some corrections to it. After some years, the theory of a wandering star around the sun started getting acceptance. The theory was called Binary Theories.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • In 1943, Otto Schmidt propounded the interstellar dust hypothesis. He proposed that the sun, in its present form, passed through a dense interstellar cloud and emerged enveloped in a cloud of dust and gas. Otto Schmidt of Russia and Carl Weizsacker of Germany revised the Nebular Hypothesis.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                They believed dust like ‘Solar Nebula’ with heavy helium and hydrogen surrounds the sun. A disk-shaped cloud was created by the friction of particles in the solar Nebula. The planet was formed due to the accretion process.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                • In modern times the most accepted theory regarding the origin of Universe is the Big Bang Theory also known as expanding Universe Theory. Universal expansion was proved by Edwin Hubble in 1920. According to the Big Bang Theory, a violent explosion of a tiny body occurred which resulted in huge expansion and the change of some particles into an energy form. Due to this expansion, some energy got converted into matter. This happened 13.7/13.8 billion years ago.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Another proof of this Edwin Hubble concluded that galaxies are drifting apart. This is important observational evidence consistent with the hypothesis of an expanding Universe. After initial expansion, the universe cooled sufficiently to allow the formation of subatomic particles and later simple atoms. Giant clouds of these elements later combined due to gravity eventually forming early stars and galaxies. The galaxies further broke down resulting in the formation of stars and stars broke down (ran out of fuel) resulting in the formation of early planets.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • In 1907 John Joly, used his knowledge of mineralogy to figure out the age of different minerals. According to him certain rock-forming minerals were often characterized by the presence of small circular dark spots or concentric rings. He called it the Mineral Halo.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Professor H.H. Russell used Uranium –Lead and Thorium-Lead to determine the age of Earth. According to it the age of our planet is 2 billion and 25 crore years and 4 billion and 60 crore year old respectively.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Radiometric dating has proven to be the most successful way offiguring out the Earth’s age. As Uranium and Thorium are found in one form or the other in different quantities in every rock formation, the Uranium Dating Technique to determine the age of Earth becomes very useful.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                The Earth · The Geological History: key facts from the book
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Geological History of Earth follows the major events in Earth’s past based on the geological time scale. The first efforts to understand the Geological History of Earth were made by a French naturalist Comte de Buffon. At present the geological time scale is used, which is a system of chronological dating that relates geological states to time.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • The primary defined divisions of time are eons. Eons are divided into eras which are in turn divided into periods and epochs.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Pre Cambrian Era – Earth was initially molten due to extreme volcanism and frequent collisions with other bodies. Water began accumulating in the atmosphere. The only flora present at this time was seagrasses. In the warm oceans emergence of spineless creatures also took place.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                A geological period is one of the several subdivisions of geological time. Every period is named after its characteristic events.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                (1) Cambrian Period – The waters of the Cambrian period appear to have been widespread and shallow. The seas saw the emergence of creatures with spinal cord along with spinal cord during this period.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                (2) Ordovician Period – By this time process of mountain formation had started and thus period witnessed heavy volcanic activity. Flora and fauna were only limited to the seas.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                (3) Silurian Period – The period witnessed the emergence of terrestrial flora however leaf formation was yet not present. Diversity in the species of flora was also seen. A very prominent phenomenon of this period was large scale development and expansion of coral reefs.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                (4) Devonian Period - The period was a time of great tectonic activity as a result of which it witnessed large scale mountain formations and volcanic activities. Various varieties of Fish emerged and evolved during this period, hence the period is also known as the ‘Age of Fishes’.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                (5) Carboniferous period – Our Earth is made up of different plates. These plates are not stationary but keep moving because of tectonic activity. Hence, these plates are responsible for shifting of the continents and oceanic floors into various parts of the planet. The Carboniferous was a time of active mountain building, as the supercontinent Pangea came together. The supercontinent was surrounded by a large water body. The sea was named Panthalassa by Wegener. The northern part of Pangea i.e. Laurasia (North America, Europe and Asia) and southern part Gondwana (South America, Africa, Madagascar, Peninsular India, Australia and Antarctica).

                                                                                                                                                                                                                (6) Permian Period – During this period, because of geological turmoil, the birth of high mountain ranges was seen in Europe, Asia and Eastern United States of America (Appalachian). Another factor witnessed was the increase in terrestrial species.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                (7) Triassic Period – The period witnessed the emergence of carnivorous aquatic reptiles that had a resemblance to and characteristics of fishes. The period also witnessed the first evolution of terrestrial mammals. Flies and termites also came into the picture during this period along with the origin of dinosaurs.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                (8) Jurassic Period – This period saw the development of the size and diversity of terrestrial reptiles. Some aerial birds such as Archaeopteryx also emerged during this period. This period was dominated by dinosaurs.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Archaeological evidence of dinosaurs in India has been found at Raiyoli in Mahisagar district of Gujarat and in Bara Simla Hills near the rivers Narmada in Jabalpur district of Madhya Pradesh.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                (9) Cretaceous Period – Geological developments and transformations were very active during this period. As a result the Rocky Mountains, Andes Mountain ranges of Europe and Isthmus of Panama were formed.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                The tertiary period has been categorized into different epochs. They are as follows -

                                                                                                                                                                                                                (1) Palaeocene Epoch

                                                                                                                                                                                                                (2) Eocene Epoch – The epoch saw the formation of the Indian Ocean, Atlantic Ocean and the Himalayan orogeny.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                (3) Oligocene Epoch - The epoch witnessed expansion of land mass. Geological activity continued in Europe and America and the formation of Alps started.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                (4) Miocene Epoch – The epoch witnessed a lot of geological activity as a result of which Alps mountain range was formed, there was an uplift in the height of the lesser Himalayas and Greater Himalayas.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                (5) Pliocene Epoch – The North Sea, Black Sea, Arabian Sea and Caspian Sea were formed the formation of the Shiwalik range also took place during this epochs.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Quaternary Period - has been divided into two Epochs Pleistocene Epoch and Holocene Epochs.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Pleistocene Epoch - The Pleistocene Epoch is defined as the time period that began nearly 2.0 million years ago and lasted until about 10,000 years ago. The most recent ice age occurred then. Almost all the continents experienced glacier formation. The ice-sheets spread was categorized into four different times. Hence, sub-ice ages have been classified and named according to their area of occurrence. They are as follows –

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Nebraskan, Kansan Illinois, Iowa and Wisconsin in North America. Similarly, Albrecht Penck and Eduard Bruckner classified the ice ages of Europe. They are as follows – Gunz, Mindel, Riss, Wurm.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Holocene Epoch – The Holocene Epoch began 10,000 years ago.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • The melting of ice sheet led to reemergence and expansion of forests in Europe. Aquatic flora and fauna evolved into their present biological characteristics.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • The period between 1300 to 1870 A.D. is known as the Little Ice Age. During this time Europe and North America were much colder as compared to the 20th century.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                Rocks: key facts from the book

                                                                                                                                                                                                                The Earth's crust is made up of rocks. A rock is a naturally occurring solid aggregate of one or more minerals or mineraloids, and it may also contain glass rock fragments, fossils, or organic matter such as plant material in coal. Petrology is the study of rocks, which is an essential component of geology.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                • The major groups of rocks are defined as igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Igneous Rocks – Igneous rock is formed through the cool ing and solidification of magma or lava. They are granular in texture and are not found in the stratified form. They are devoid of any kind of fossils. Igneous rocks often have a correlation with volcanic activities. Igneous rocks are hard for water to penetrate. Igneous rock is found both in crystalline and non-crystalline form. They are also known as primary rocks. Igneous rocks are divided into two main categories-

                                                                                                                                                                                                                (a) Plutonic or intrusive rocks – formed when magma cools and crystallises slowly within the earth’s crust. Ex.-granite, gabbros and pegmatite.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                (b) Volcanic or extrusive rocks are – Basalt, volcanic breccias etc.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Sedimentary rocks – Sedimentary rocks are formed at the Earth’s surface by the accumulation and cementation of fragments of earlier rocks, minerals and organisms or as chemical precipitates and organic growth in water (sedimentation).

                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Sediments are formed by the weathering of earlier rocks (igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic) by erosion from a source and are then transported to the place of deposition by water, wind, ice and mass movement of glaciers (agents of denudation). After this through the process of lithification, loose, unconsolidated sediments are turned into solid sedimentary rocks.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Many sedimentary rocks are able to retain their specific characteristics in their depository layer, even after lithification. It is the reason why sand stones have multiple layers of different concentrations.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Sedimentary rocks are formed by the accumulation of sediments. There are three basic types of sedimentary rocks-

                                                                                                                                                                                                                (i) Sedimentary rocks formed as a result of mechanical processes- Ex - sandstones, shale, conglomerate etc.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                (ii) sedimentary rocks - limestone, coal, etc.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                (iii) Chemical sedimentary rocks - halite, potassium and magnesium salt etc.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Metamorphic Rocks – These rocks are formed by subjecting any rock type – sedimentary rock or igneous rock to different temperature and pressure conditions and chemical processes than those in which the original rock was formed. This process is called metamorphism meaning “change of form”. The result is a profound change in physical properties and chemistry of the stone. The temperature and pressure required for this process are always higher than those found at the Earth’s surface.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Metamorphosed form of Igneous Rocks –

                                                                                                                                                                                                                (1) Granite – Gneiss

                                                                                                                                                                                                                (2) Basalt – Schist

                                                                                                                                                                                                                (3) Basalt – Amphibolite

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Metamorphosed form of Sedimentary Rocks -

                                                                                                                                                                                                                (1) Shale – Slate

                                                                                                                                                                                                                (2) Limestone – Marble

                                                                                                                                                                                                                (3) Chalk and Dolomite – Marble

                                                                                                                                                                                                                (4) Sandstone – Quartzite

                                                                                                                                                                                                                (5) Conglomerate - Gneiss

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Metamorphosed form of Metamorphic Rocks –

                                                                                                                                                                                                                (1) Slate – Phyllite

                                                                                                                                                                                                                (2) Phyllite – Schist

                                                                                                                                                                                                                (3) Gabbro – Serpentine

                                                                                                                                                                                                                The Volcano: key facts from the book
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • A volcano is a rupture in the crust of a planetary mass object, such as Earth, that allows hot lava, volcanic ash and gases to escape from a magma chamber below the surface.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Among the gases emitted through a volcanic eruption the, highest quantity is that of water vapor (H₂O). Other gases emitted are carbon-dioxide (CO₂), sulphur dioxide (SO₂), hydrogen (H₂), carbon-monoxide (CO), hydrogen chloride (HCl), hydrogen fluoride (HF) and helium (He). Magma is made of molten rock and is stored in the Earth’s interior. lava is magma that reaches the Earth's surface with temperature ranging from about 600°C 1200°C. When Lava reaches the surface it cools to form igneous rocks. The composition of almost all lava of the earth’s crust is dominated by silica (SiO₂) materials. Based on the silicate, lava can be classified into two types- Acidic Lava and Basic Lava.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Acidic lava is highly dense and sticky in nature and has high silica content. Basic lava, on the other hand is less dense and has low silica content.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Intrusive igneous rocks are formed when lava cools and solidifies before reaching the earth’s surface. Igneous rocks are of two types – intrusive and extrusive.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Caldera is an extended version of a volcanic vent.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • A geyser is a spring characterized by intermittent discharge of water ejected turbulently and accompanied by steam. Generally, all Geyser field sites are located near the active volcanic areas, and the geyser effect is due to the proximity of magma. For example the Old Faithful Geyser of Yellowstone National Park in the United States of America.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • A fumarole is the last phase in a volcanic activity. It is an opening that emits steam and gases. The name solfatara is given to fumarole that emit sulfurous gases. Mount Katmai of Alaska (USA) is known as the Valley of Ten Thousand Smokes. Volcanoes are categorized according to their level of activeness–

                                                                                                                                                                                                                (1) Active Volcano – An active volcano has its vent open and keeps emitting smoke, gas and lava often. At present Mount Kilauea is the one of the world's most active volcano. Situated on Hawaiian Islands of the USA it has been in an active state from between 1983 to 2018.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                • The top three most active volcanoes are – Kilauea, Mount Etna and Piton de la Fournaise.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • On the basis of size, the largest active volcano on Earth is Mauna Loa, situated on Hawaiian Islands. Mount Etna is an active volcano on the east coast of the island of Sicily in Italy. It stands 3357 meters tall.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Stromboli is an active volcano on Stromboli Island, north of Sicily in the Tyrrhenian Sea. The volcano has erupted many times and is constantly active with minor eruptions, often visible from many points on the island and from the surrounding sea, giving rise to Island’s nickname “Lighthouse of the Mediterranean.”
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Nevados Ojos del Salado is an active volcano in the Andes on the Argentina Chile border and the highest active volcano in the world at 6879 m.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Mount Erebus is an active volcano located on Ross Island in Antarctica.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Barren Island is an island located in the Andaman Sea, dominated by Barren Volcano, the only confirmed active volcano in South Asia.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Mount Fuji located on Honshu Island in an active volcano in Japan. Presently Mount Vesuvius (Italy) is an a active volcano. Mount St. Helens is a volcano located in Skamania County, Washington, in the Pacific Northwest region of the United States. It is also known as the 'Fujiyama of America'.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                (2) Dormant Volcanoes- A dormant volcano is one that has not erupted recently but is expected to do so again. Kilimanjaro volcano of Tanzania. It has three main volcanic cones- Kibo, Mawenzi and Shira. Among these peaks Kibo is dormant while Mawenzi and Shira are extinct. Damavand of Iran.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                (3) Extinct Volcano – Extinct volcanoes are those that scientist consider unlikely to erupt again because the volcano no longer has a magma supply. For example- Kulal (Kenya) in Africa and Koh-e-Sultan of Pakistan.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                The Earthquake: key facts from the book
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • An earthquake is the shaking of the surface of the Earth, resulting from the sudden release of energy in the earth’s lithosphere that creates seismic waves. An earthquake's point of initial rupture is called its seismic focus or hypocenter. The epicenter is the point at ground level directly above the hypocenter. The epicenter is the point on the Earth's surface directly above the hypocenter. All natural earthquakes occur in the lithosphere. There are three basic types of seismic waves –

                                                                                                                                                                                                                (1) Primary Waves (P-wave) – They are similar to sound waves. They are also known as longitudinal waves. P-waves travel faster than any other waves. Their intensity of travel depends upon the density of the rock they encounter. Since they are the fastest traveling seismic wave, they are the first signal from an earthquake to arrive at any affected location or at a seismograph. P–waves may be transmitted through gases, liquids and solids.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                (2) Secondary Waves (S-waves) – They are similar to light waves. They are also known as transverse waves. These waves arrive after the primary waves and travel slower than the P-waves. The S-waves can travel only through solid materials.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                (3) Surface Waves (L-waves) – These waves travel slower than the other two waves and can travel only through the surface of the earth. Surface waves travel around the globe before reaching the epicenter. Surface waves are the most damaging of all the waves. Surface waves are of two types

                                                                                                                                                                                                                (i) Love waves (ii) Rayleigh waves. In these two waves Love waves have higher speed.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                • The magnitude of an earthquake is the indication of the energy released.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • The magnitude of the earthquake is measured on the Richter scale and intensity on Mercalli scale. The Richter scale was invented in the year 1935 by Charles Francis Richter. The Richter scale is a logarithmic scale whose base is 10. Each step represents a ten-fold increase in amplitude on the seismogram, whereas in terms of energy, each whole number increase corresponds to an increase of about 32 times (31.6) the amount of energy released. Every point on the scale (earthquake waves) denotes an energy release, equivalent to 6 ounces of TNT (Trinitrotoluene).
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Seismometer is used to measure earthquake waves. The term tsunami is borrowed from the Japanese meaning harbor wave.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Tsu means Harbor and nami means waves. Tsunami is caused by earthquakes, volcanic eruptions and other underwater explosions and their destructive power can be enormous affecting entire ocean basins.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • The Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear disaster was an nuclear accident at the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant initiated primarily by a tsunami following an earthquake on 11 March 2011. It led to a nuclear meltdown and the release of radioactivity in the area.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • The Ring of Fire is a major area in the basin of the Pacific Ocean where many earthquakes and volcanic eruptions occur. The Ring of Fire is sometimes called Circum Pacific belt. About 90% of the world’s earthquakes occur along the Ring of Fire.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • There are four main conditions for the occurrence of earthquakes in this region – (1) Point of interaction between sea and land (2) Young fold mountainous region (3) Volcanic Activity (4) Plate tectonics – movement and collision of plates.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • The region consists of Chile, California, Alaska, Japan, Philippines, New Zealand etc.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • The Northwestern part of the India subcontinent is an earthquake prone area. This is because it is the convergence zone of Indian and Eurasian tectonic plates.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                • The earthquake-prone regions of India are included in the Mid-Continental Belt. The Belt starts from Cape Verde and includes Atlantic Ocean, Mediterranean Sea, and young fold mountain ranges like the Alps, Caucasus and Himalayas. The Mid-Atlantic Belt is a mid ocean belt.

Tidal → James Jeans, Harold Jeffreys. Nova → F. Hoyle, Littleton.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Folding (mountain building) → orogenic force, from interaction of tectonic plates.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Which of the following processes do not come under diastrophism?—

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Diastrophism → slow or sudden movements of the crust by internal forces (e.g. earthquakes); heterogenic processes do not come under it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Consider the following:1,2,3,4,5 and 6

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Dynamic changes on Earth's surface → all six: electromagnetic radiation, geothermal energy, gravitational force, plate movements, rotation and revolution of the Earth.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Chronological order: Sihawal (Lower Palaeolithic) → Patpara (Middle Palaeolithic) → Baghor (Upper Palaeolithic) → Khetaunhi (Neolithic, Microlithic). Code 4, 1, 3, 2.

The book's own order differs.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Rajasthan desert or Thar desert is the expanse of which of the following?Pleistocene and recent deposits

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Thar (Rajasthan) desert → Pleistocene and recent deposits; began forming about 70,000 years ago. Pleistocene: 2 million to 10,000 years ago (NCERT).

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Which type of rock is formed from cooling and solidification of lava?Igneous

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Igneous rock → cooling and solidification of magma/lava. Extrusive (on the surface, e.g. basalt); intrusive (inside the crust, e.g. granite).

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Consider the following statements about the sedimentary rocks:1, 2, 3 and 4

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Sedimentary rocks → formed at the surface from weathered older rocks and remains; contain fossils; occur in layers (strata). All four statements true.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Full question and explanation · 2 paper(s)

                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Sandstone is flaky rock, because –It is formed underwater

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Sandstone is layered ('flaky') because it forms underwater (sea or low-lying areas); a sedimentary rock that changes into quartzite.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Consider the following statements:Only one of the Statements II and III is correct and that explains Statement I.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Chalk → porous and permeable (II true, explains I). Clay → highly porous but least permeable, so 'clay is not at all porous' (III) is false.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Which statement of the following is true for igneous rocks?They are both crystal and non-crystal

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Igneous rocks → both crystalline and non-crystalline; made of silicate minerals; no fossils or layers; supply little water.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Which of the following rocks is not likely to contain fossils?Granite

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Granite (igneous, plutonic/intrusive) does not contain fossils; conglomerate, sandstone and shale are sedimentary rocks, which contain fossils.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Origin of Metamorphic rocks occurs from …….. rock?Both Igneous and Sedimentary

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Metamorphic rocks → formed from either igneous or sedimentary rocks by heat and pressure ('metamorphism' = change of form, Greek).

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Which one of the following is not an example of Metamorphic rock?Granite

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Granite is igneous, not metamorphic. Metamorphic pairs: granite → gneiss; basalt → schist/amphibolite; shale → slate; limestone → marble; sandstone → quartzite.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Which one of the following is not associated with the 'group'?Gneiss

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Odd one out → gneiss (metamorphic, usually from granite); sandstone, limestone and shale are sedimentary.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Consider the following statements:Both Statement-II and Statement-III are correct and both of them explain Statement-I

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Rainfall weathers rock: dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid (carbonation, active in limestone) and dissolved oxygen causes oxidation (rust). II and III true, both explain I.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Consider the following:All four

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Volcanic products → lava, pyroclastic debris, volcanic bombs, ash and dust, gases (nitrogen and sulphur compounds; a little chlorine, hydrogen, argon). All four listed are.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Which of the following is a Basic landform?Volcanic cone

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Basic landform → volcanic cone (lava piled around the vent); residual mountains, monadnocks and erosional waterfalls are products of erosion.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                                                                                                                                                                                                • The most abundant gas emitted from volcanoes is –Water Vapour

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Most abundant volcanic gas → water vapour (H2O); next CO2 and SO2; also H2S, H2, CO, HCl, HF, He.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Which one of the following is the highest volcanic mountain in the world?Mount Cotopaxi

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Highest volcano among the options → Mount Cotopaxi (5911 m); Kilimanjaro 5881 m, Pinatubo 1486 m, Tall 311 m (Philippines).

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                                                                                                                                                                                                • In which belt, the volcanic eruption is maximum?Circumpacific

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Most volcanic eruptions → Circum-Pacific belt ('Ring of Fire'): about 75 percent of active volcanoes and most earthquakes.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                                                                                                                                                                                                • The molten material found inside the earth is calledNone of the above

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Molten rock inside the Earth → magma (not lava, basalt or obsidian), so 'None of the above'. Ejected magma = lava; acidic lava is viscous, basic lava fluid.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Don't confuse Magma is inside the Earth; the same material is called lava once it comes out.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Rock formed inside the Earth as a result of solidification of lava is called –Plutonic rocks

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Magma solidified deep below the surface → plutonic rocks (slow cooling, large crystals); hypabyssal rocks form at intermediate depth.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Volcanic eruptions do not occur in the:Baltic Sea

                                                                                                                                                                                                                No volcanic eruptions in the Baltic Sea (not at a plate edge); volcanoes occur at converging or diverging plate edges.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Mt. Etna is –A volcano

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Mount Etna → active volcano on the east coast of Sicily, Italy (about 3357 m).

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Where is the mount Saint Helens situated?United State of America

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Mount Saint Helens → active strato-volcano in Washington, USA (Pacific North West); called the 'Fujiyama of America'.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Mauna Loa ('Long Mountain') → active volcano covering half of Hawaii Island, USA; first well-documented eruption in 1843. Must know

                                                                                                                                                                                                                Mauna Loa (Hawaii, US) → world's largest volcano; erupted in 2022, first time in 38 years. Name means 'Long Mountain'; above-sea part extends about 120 km.
